Library closures, pool charges and Te Papa funding cuts proposed as Wellington City Council prepares for rates capping

New Zealand Herald October 05, 2026

Swimming pools, libraries, and Te Papa are in the firing line as Wellington City Council proposes sweeping service cuts. Photo / Mark Mitchell

Wellington City Council is eyeing sweeping service cuts in order to meet looming rates caps, with proposals to slash funding to Te Papa, shut community libraries, and phase out school swimming subsidies.

Deputy Mayor Ben McNulty is leading the cost-cutting initiative, and said the council needs to find $60 million of savings in order to comply with the 4% rates cap due to begin in 2029.

The council’s revenue and financial value working group has this morning unveiled its first tranche of proposed cuts, totalling $25m in slashed services and extra charges.

“None of this is easy,” McNulty told the Herald, saying councillors aim to trim as much as possible while still protecting frontline services.

“There will be some [residents] very unhappy that we’re looking at any type of spending reductions whatsoever,” he said.

“There will be others [who] would want to see the council slash and burn down to the ground.”

Decisions will be made through the council’s Long-term Plan next year, with the public expected to be consulted on proposals in March or April, before the 10-year plan is adopted in late June, McNulty said.

Te Papa, New Zealand’s national museum, is predominantly funded by central Government, as well as donations and commercial revenue, but also receives $1.8m per year from the council.

That annual funding is facing the axe in the council’s proposal with majority support for a partial or staged reduction.

It comes as the celebrated museum is struggling, with recent moves to start charging international visitors not saving it from multimillion-dollar annual losses and a recent restructure spelling layoffs.

Wellington Museum and City Gallery are also in the firing line, with recommendations that they be closed on Mondays, excluding public holidays, or remaining open for cruise ship passengers with a new visitor charge.

WellingtonNZ, the capital’s economic development agency tasked with promoting the city to tourists and businesses, is facing a $1m cut to its annual grant.

The city’s annual New Year’s Eve festivities, which feature fireworks, live music and food-trucks, would be cancelled, saving ratepayers a potential $290,000.

A majority in the working group also support a “no new playgrounds” policy for the next 10 years.

The city’s council-run swimming pools are also in the firing line, with recommendations to allow only one adult free supervision per child under-8, and additional supervising adults to be charged a full swim fee.

School swim subsidies face being phased out progressively, saving up to $120,000 per year.

Library cuts were discussed with options including closing some branches, reducing opening days or hours at under-used libraries, staff cuts and bringing back fees and charges.

The working group decided on a full review into the cost effectiveness and efficiency of the city’s libraries.

Cuts to spending on library collections and online databases are also proposed.

To increase revenue, parking charges could be increased through demand-based pricing and leasing or selling off road space.

The only recommendation that would increase spending concerned resilience and hazard work, which McNulty said related to climate infrastructure, and follows April floods.

Read the council’s full list of suggested cuts here.

The Government’s rates-capping legislation sets an initial 2–4% target range for annual council rates increases, with a 4% cap taking effect in 2029.

But councils have been told they must consider the 4% caps from July 1, 2027, when preparing their long-term plans.

Water charges are excluded, and councils can seek exemptions for exceptional circumstances, including natural disasters or prudent financial-management reasons.

Local Government Minister Simon Watts said that for too long ratepayers “have been hit with steep and unexpected rates increases”, citing median rises across the country of 14.2% and 9.2% in the last two years.

Minister Chris Bishop has said the policy aimed to prevent excessive council spending on non-essentials: “it’s a policy against $2.3 million for light-up public toilets in Wellington”, he told Parliament in August.

However, uncertainty remains over the reforms, with the Local Government (Rates Capping) Amendment Bill not passed in Parliament.

It is at the select committee stage and is expected to be discussed next term.

DoC launches early-warning tool to stop weeds before they get started

New Zealand Herald October 05, 2026

DoC scientist Dr Kate McAlpine with some of the weeds she has been battling. Photo / RNZ, Phil Pennington

By Phil Pennington of RNZ

Raising the alarm early about new or fast-spreading weeds is now easier and faster, with a new Department of Conservation (DoC) digital surveillance tool.

DoC is launching a new free digital surveillance tool today that might have been able to stop tradescantia (Wandering Willie) back in the day, or at least increase the chances.

The tool’s creator believes the Smart Weed Alert Tool – or Swat – can put a big dent in the country’s billion-dollar weed control problem.

“There’ll be a lot of users, and there’ll be a lot of new weeds that people learn about - sometimes they might wish they didn’t,” Dr Kate McAlpine from DoC said.

“It will stop the next massive weed before it gets established.”

McAlpine was at an AI hackathon several years ago when they asked for ideas to turn into tech tools.

She had been thinking about weeds – her PhD subject – and the extremely high toll they took on farms, forestry and native species.

Three years, $1 million and input from many smart people later, she is launching Swat.

Next week she will be at global climate change talks in Armenia, where the tool has won a coveted spot at a biodiversity expo.

“The whole world is already interested.

“Yeah, going global a little bit earlier than I had intended, but just way too good an opportunity ... Week two!”

“Thousands of plant observations are recorded every day, but no one has the time to manually search through them all for signs of emerging weed threats,” McAlpine said.

“Swat does that automatically, alerting people when something important turns up.”

At the top of Rolleston St, a steep climb from downtown Wellington, McAlpine was recently searching through road reserve banks thick with weeds.

“Probably at least 10 major environmental weeds on this bank ... It’s probably double that, to be honest.

“We’ve got arum lily, we’ve got pampas, we’ve got brush wattle, English ivy ... liquorice bush down the road a bit.”

Liquorice bush does not taste or smell like liquorice, but McAlpine said it was nastier than that.

“It’s an emerging weed, actually. Just one of those species that’s been sitting in New Zealand for probably decades, just starting to turn up in the wild.”

There are 25,000 other exotic plants like that in New Zealand gardens, where any one of them might escape and start invading.

The open-source digital surveillance system is an early warning system for new weeds and weed spread.

With Swat anyone can set up a highly customised set of alerts for types of weeds and the places they are found.

The tool will then continually scan local and international databases, including the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, for when people find them.

“Swat can tell that that’s the first record of that species for the region, or the suburb, or the country, or the island, and will ... send anyone who’s got an alert set up with those criteria to say ‘hey, this is the first record for this island or suburb’,” McAlpine said.

There has been a positive reaction to the prototype, McAlpine said.

“Several councils have said ‘hey, this is amazing’. We just found out about two historical populations that we didn’t already know about.”

Te Papa curator of botany Leon Perrie was alerted by the prototype to a nasty little fern in northern wetlands that popped up recently in Taranaki.

“The thing is, it’s not meant to be there,” Perrie said.

“At the museum, I’m interested in documenting them.

“So ultimately, sure, we want to get rid of the weeds, but it’s a chance to collect a specimen of things that are maybe newly present in the country or in the region.”

Others who received alerts, such as community groups, might choose to root out the weeds, or prioritise other invasive species to tackle that Swat – with its highly detailed, zoom-in-able maps – showed were a bigger problem in their locale.

It can tell them if there was a bio-agent that worked on that pest.

Anybody who has been using plant-spotting sites like iNaturalist will automatically add to the dots on the maps at Swat, making the weed alerts more accurate.

In Waikato, the prototype found six historical infestations the regional council was not aware of.

“You may have just notified us about a serious potential weed on our doorstep!” council pest plants expert Heidi Pene told McAlpine.

“It’s proven its worth already.”

Of particular interest was a historical broom corn millet site very near the northern boundary where agricultural machinery crosses from Auckland to Waikato.

Swat also alerted it to eel grass, field horsetail, variegated thistle and marshwort sites to follow up.

The historical tabs in the maps taught the council about herbarium records dating back to 1939.

“We had no idea they’d been around that long,” Pene said.

“This looks like a fabulous tool with wonderful potential.”

AI helped build Swat quickly and relatively cheaply through the Govtech Accelerator programme, which aims to use start-up tech to solve a public problem.

The direct cost of weed control, such as cutting out wilding pines, to councils, DoC and others is put at $50m a year.

McAlpine hopes the tool can make like a weed and spread quickly.

“Because nobody’s got enough resources to be doing regular or systematic surveillance.

“There’s a lot of power in this.”

Police have completed a forensic examination of a Linwood property linked to missing Christchurch father Braydon Hepworth, but are providing few details about the investigation as inquiries continue into his disappearance.

As the 21-year-old’s family make increasingly desperate appeals for information about the missing man, police will not be drawn on whether they suspect foul play is involved.

To date, the last confirmed sighting of Hepworth was at a Linwood service station on September 3.

Security footage showed him wearing a Monster Energy-branded beanie with a pair of headphones over the top.

Police first appealed for help to find Hepworth on September 23 after he was reported missing.

On Friday, they issued a fresh appeal for information and confirmed they were searching a property in Linwood in connection with his disappearance.

The house is located on the corner of Hereford and England Sts and police said it was believed to be Hepworth’s last known address.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

It is understood the house runs as a backpackers of sorts and has several residents of varying lengths of stay.

During the search, police cordoned off the corner property, which has caravans at the back.

Officers stood guard outside while investigators worked

“Staff have made extensive inquiries to date, and Braydon has not been located. We are very concerned for Braydon,” police said in a statement.

“Police continue to appeal for anybody with information regarding Braydon’s whereabouts to please get in contact with us.

“Police and Braydon’s family have serious concerns for his wellbeing, as this is extremely out of character for him.”

Yesterday police refused to comment on the status of the investigation, including who Hepworth last spoke to or contacted, when he last accessed his bank accounts or used his phone, if he has accessed medication he uses daily, whether they believe the young father has been a victim of foul play, and if so, whether any persons of interest had been identified.

This morning Detective Senior Sergeant Karen Simmons issued a statement.

“A scene examination at the address believed to be Braydon’s last known address has now been completed,” she said.

“The operation to understand the circumstances surrounding his disappearance remains ongoing.

“Police continue to appeal for anybody with information regarding Braydon’s whereabouts to please get in contact with us.”

Hepworth’s mother, Char Huntley, has been appealing for information on Facebook since September 22.

“Please help me keep looking for my boy … Braydon Hepworth. He’s 21 and Type 1 diabetic. He needs insulin daily to stay alive,” she wrote four days later.

“This is devastating, not knowing where he is, if he is safe, if he needs help but can’t get it, if he is still in Christchurch or has gone further willingly or not.

“He has a 9-month-old daughter and two siblings as well. He’s loved and very missed by many, and we are all concerned for his health and wellbeing. He is not in any trouble; we just need him home.”

Huntley revealed that as of August 4, Hepworth had “a month’s worth” of insulin.

“So we are desperately needing to find him to help him,” she said.

She had called hospitals “all over the South Island” as well as bus, shuttle and ferry companies in case Hepworth was sick, injured or had travelled away from Christchurch.

“Have been in the city where he would frequent and been showing his photo in multiple shops. No luck,” she said.

“Messaged friends and our extended family that know him or he may go to. No luck.

“His phone is off and all social media are non-active and everything is only delivered but not received his end. This is unnaturally out of character for him to not be heard from for this long. I am very scared for his safety, and the not knowing is the worst.”

Huntley said she was in a situation “no parent should ever go through”.

“I won’t stop looking until I find him safe… I am heartbroken not knowing where he is,” she updated later in September.

“His health and safety is a serious concern. Someone must know something that will lead to his location. Please help me find him. I love him, and I need him home.”

In her most recent update last week, 27 days after the last confirmed sighting of Hepworth, she begged anyone with information to “please speak up”.

“Remain anonymous if you need, but let me get my son back safe,” she said.

“Our family is broken with the uncertainty of his whereabouts and well-being. We have searched many places, made multiple calls and have no solid leads yet. I’m needing any information leading to his discovery.”

The grandfather of Hepworth’s daughter also posted online urging people to come forward with any information that could help the family.

“Although Braydon is not my biological son, he was in a relationship with our daughter and they have a beautiful 9-month-old daughter together. From the very first day we met Braydon, he called us Mum and Dad, and we called him our son. Over time, we built a very strong bond with him, and he has become an important part of our family,” he wrote.

“I received a message from Braydon on 2 September telling me that he was planning to get his car licence and was also sorting out other appointments. He had been doing so well, which is why everything that has happened over the past few weeks is so concerning and completely out of character for him.

“The search will continue, and we are asking everyone to please keep sharing the missing-person posts and keep an eye out for Braydon.”

He thanked everyone who had supported Hepworth’s family during “an extremely difficult and stressful time” and helped to search for him and spread the word about his disappearance.

“It truly means more to us than we can put into words,” he said.

“Thank you from the bottom of our hearts for continuing to support Braydon, our family and especially his little daughter during this incredibly difficult time.

“We are desperately hoping and praying that we receive good news soon.”

Over the weekend, he posted a message directly to Hepworth, revealing he had spent “countless hours driving and walking around looking for him”.

“I’m just lost for words, Braydon - please let us know where you are. You’re not in trouble; we all just want you back home,” he wrote.

It is unclear if Hepworth was working at the time he went missing.

In June 2025, he posted on Facebook looking for fulltime work “urgently”.

If you have seen Hepworth or know his whereabouts or movements, please call the police non-emergency number 105 and reference file number 260918/8420.

New Zealand police are investigating the time spent here by the co-pilot accused of attacking a flydubai captain with an emergency axe in an attempt to seize control of the aircraft.

Assistant Commissioner Michael Johnson confirmed to the Herald co-pilot Hammam al-Hammami had been in New Zealand, but would not reveal when he was here, for how long, or what he did while here.

“Police are aware the co-pilot spent time in New Zealand, and we are looking into the time he spent here, alongside other agencies where appropriate,” Johnson said in a statement this evening.

“We are unable to comment further at this time.”

The Civil Aviation Authority has been approached for comment.

Minister in charge of aviation James Meager told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast, “We train quite a number of international pilots in New Zealand… so it’s not surprising a few come through New Zealand, but I don’t know anything more than that.”

Spokespeople for the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment and for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade said police were the lead agency and referred questions to them.

Last Wednesday (local time), the flight’s Indian captain Smit Machchhar was assaulted allegedly by al-Hammami but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and force an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

“The co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist act” and had “attacked the captain in the cockpit with the emergency axe and tried to take control of the aircraft”, WAM quoted UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi as saying, referring to initial findings of the investigation.

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

Passengers described rushing the cockpit and a fight for control after the plane plummeted, losing around 5180m (17,000ft) of altitude in the span of a minute, according to the Flightradar24 website.

A number of Australian agencies are also probing al-Hammami’s connections to the country.

He had been granted an Australian student visa in 2014, before arriving in the country to commence a university course the following year, the Guardian reported.

Sydney Morning Herald reported he had been enrolled at RMIT University in Melbourne. CNN, reported his now-deleted LinkedIn profile said he had studied engineering.

He reportedly left Australia in 2017, and his visa was cancelled in 2019.

The Australian federal police said the Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - which included the AFP, Victoria Police and the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation - were looking into al-Hammami’s links to the country.

This man is a hero. Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian captain of flydubai Flight 1073, fought back after being stabbed in the cockpit. Despite being severely injured, he managed to unlock the cockpit door - allowing Israeli passengers and the Emirati crew to intervene and save… pic. twitter. com/x4W3mtQkag

It was revealed on Thursday, Captain Machchhar, who has been hailed as a hero for his actions, had also spent time in New Zealand, training with Mainland Air in Dunedin from 2008 to 2009.

Mainland Air chief executive Philip Kean said Machchhar remained as a recruitment agent based in India.

Kean described Machchhar as an “above average” pilot.

“He was a bit of a livewire … it’s just horrific. The main thing is that he’s still alive.

“It’s a long way to drop. It’s lucky it didn’t fall apart; those pilots did a great job at recovering the plane.”

Machchhar has described how the attack unfolded, saying the assailant hit him in the back of the head after asking for time to pray, as devout Muslims do five times a day.

“My first thought was that there was catastrophic damage to the aircraft and something is not right,” he said.

“But then after that the blows kept coming one after the other. That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

While saying his memory was not entirely clear due to his injury, Machchhar said he managed to pull open the cockpit door “but I think he shut it back closed”.

“I had that one last fight left in me,” Machchhar explained, saying he knew he faced certain death if not.

“That’s when I pushed against everything.”

The co-pilot is in custody in the UAE.

In another update this morning, multiple international news outlets have reported Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport may have been al-Hammami’s target.

CNN reported the alleged hijacker “likely wanted to target Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport” according to an Israeli official and an Israeli source familiar with the matter.

“Israel’s Channel 12 News first reported that Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport may have been the target of the hijacking,” the article read.

While BBC has said Israeli investigators believed the attacker had originally planned a hijacking for July but postponed it, “possibly because a friend was among the crew”.

Multiple media outlets have said al-Hammami had been banned from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said the suspect had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination” and had attempted to crash the plane.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Omani authorities had barred the pilot from flying over suspicions he had adopted radical ideological views, citing people familiar with the matter.

CNN, citing two sources also familiar with the matter, reported that the pilot was removed from a job at Oman’s national airline last year.

Al Arabiya, citing an informed source, also reported that Omani authorities had determined the co-pilot held extremist views.

The broadcaster said he had spent time in Syria, raising concerns he may have been influenced by radical groups there.

ABC News, citing senior intelligence and law enforcement officials familiar with the investigation, reported the suspect had allegedly been found in possession of extremist materials while a trainee.

New Zealanders getting through close to 7kg of cocaine a week

New Zealand Herald October 05, 2026

New Zealanders are getting through nearly 7kg of cocaine a week. Photo / 123rf

By Keiller MacDuff of RNZ

Cheaper, more readily available cocaine, and increased social acceptance has led to a steep increase in use in less than a decade, new research shows, with New Zealanders getting through nearly 7kg of cocaine a week in the second quarter of 2026.

This was down slightly from the record figures recorded in late 2025, with police wastewater testing reporting New Zealanders were using an estimated 9.4kg of cocaine a week.

During the same period, Kiwis were also using an estimated 34.7kg of methamphetamine each week.

Cocaine has increased threefold since 2017, with the latest New Zealand Drug Trends Survey (NZDTS) showing a “steep rise”, with 31% of respondents reporting cocaine use, compared to 11% in 2017/2018.

Massey University professor Chris Wilkins, who leads the team that conducts the annual anonymous survey, said those reporting cocaine use were using it relatively infrequently – most commonly once or twice in the previous six months, though levels of weekly and monthly use had also increased.

That meant users were less likely to suffer from the worst impacts of sustained cocaine use, which could lead to the perception the drug was relatively risk-free, Wilkins said.

Combined with New Zealand being all but excluded from earlier peaks of global cocaine use such as during the 1980s, we risked being “a little naive” about the dangers of cocaine use, Wilkins said.

“Cocaine use in New Zealand is in the ‘honeymoon’ phase where use looks glamorous and consequence-free, people are yet to experience the serious addiction and social harm that is well-known in mature cocaine markets.

“We’ve missed that cultural memory of large levels of cocaine use and harm. The real risk here is that people have this kind of perception of cocaine as low harm, low risk, based on there’s no cultural history of really bad cocaine problems like you see in North America and Europe [where] there’s really a lot of evidence of high levels of addiction, some mental health problems, and longer term cardiovascular problems as well,” he said.

Once adjusted for inflation, the price of cocaine in New Zealand had dropped by almost a third between 2017 and 2026 – from $368 a gram to $247.

Lower cost, greater availability and increased social acceptance had all led to increased use, Wilkins said.

The main reason reported by cocaine users for increasing use over the previous six months was “it’s fun/nice effect”, while expense was the top reason reported for using less or quitting in the past six months.

New supply routes via the Pacific and a glut on coca production in Central America had led to the lower prices, Wilkins said.

It was likely cocaine importation had piggybacked on new routes for methamphetamine from North and Central America via Mexican drug cartels but online sales on the dark web and social media were also contributing.

Wilkins said the cartel link increased the risk that New Zealand may be susceptible to increased amounts of opioids like fentanyl arriving through the same routes.

“If you look at the last wave of the opioid epidemic - the fourth wave in North America - that was characterised by fentanyl adulterating methamphetamine and cocaine, because essentially fentanyl is much cheaper from the drug trafficker’s point of view than providing cocaine and meth so they fill it out with fentanyl.”

He said there needed to be increased vigilance at the border and in drug testing for the arrival of fentanyl.

University of Auckland senior lecturer Dr Rhys Ponton said the survey findings supported trends from wastewater testing and samples presented at drug checking clinics.

There would be an inevitable further increase in use if prices continued to drop, he said.

“This shift in the market means healthcare professionals and services working with people who use drugs will need to adapt their advice and approaches to include cocaine,” Ponton said.

He urged a harm reduction approach, including expanding access to drug checking and encouraging its use.

Auckland University of Technology Law School professor Khylee Quince said the NZDTS data confirmed the perception that cocaine was somehow “safer” and “cleaner” than other illicit substances.

“This is likely to be connected to the heavy correlation between cocaine use and socio-economic advantage and status - which may of course also be a proxy for ethnicity, that cocaine is a white drug for white people.

“Cocaine users are likely to be employed and be high earners, so this perception is a form of confirmation bias - whereby people believe information that supports their views and behaviours - cocaine is ok, but meth is not.”

Quince said easier access and falling prices meant cocaine use among Māori had almost trebled in recent years, “illustrating a probable gap between the perception and reality of who is using cocaine in Aotearoa and in what context”.

University of Wellington associate professor Dr Fiona Hutton said drug-testing service KnowYourStuffNZ had reported that cocaine made up 10% of everything tested during the 2025/26 season, up from 6% last year and 5% the previous year.

She warned against a “moral panic-type response”, and encouraged people to have illicit drugs tested, and to inform themselves about the drugs they used through sites such as the New Zealand Drug Foundation site, The Level.

Hutton said monitoring trends showed drugs and drug use fluctuated over time with new substances making their way on to the market or traditional drugs such as cocaine finding new popularity.

“Governments and policy makers should ensure those working with people who use drugs have the resourcing to support those who may have problems associated with cocaine (and other drug) use and to examine ways to effectively reduce harm, rather than focusing solely on supply side ‘war on drugs’ type responses that often cause more harm,” she said.

- RNZ

The Sandpaper series was radioactive from the start. Then a USB stick was delivered to my room

Sydney Morning Herald October 06, 2026

Australia is returning to South Africa for a Test series for the first time since the ball-tampering affair. Covering the last one in 2018 was an assignment like no other.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Sixteen days before Cameron Bancroft was caught hiding a piece of sandpaper down his pants, someone knocked on the door of my hotel room in Port Elizabeth, where the second Test between Australia and South Africa was about to begin.

It was about lunchtime, but I hadn’t ordered any food, and the housekeeping staff had already been around that morning.

Instead, as I got up and answered the door, I realised it was a delivery of another kind – a USB stick.

For a sports journalist covering cricket, this was not a common occurrence.

But a spiteful first Test in Durban in the preceding days had already given the impression this was not going to be your average tour.

On the thumb drive, as I discovered when I plugged it into my laptop, was unseen footage of an incident that had lit up the series just as it had begun – a stairwell clash between David Warner and South Africa wicketkeeper Quinton de Kock.

In a contest that was already brimming with tension, the clip showed the altercation from a different camera angle than the earlier leak to South African media and made for a fresh round of headlines.

I wasn’t to know that by the next leg of the tour in Cape Town, the vision would be rendered a footnote to one of cricket’s most infamous episodes.

Whenever I’m asked about reporting on the ball-tampering scandal of 2018 for the Herald and The Age in South Africa, I always remind people that Australia’s series there that year was already radioactive before it exploded at Newlands.

The days and weeks that followed the Australian team’s self-destruction on day three of the third Test were chaotic as Warner, Bancroft and captain Steve Smith were sent home.

In a piece in the hours after Bancroft was exposed, I said that the Cape Town affair was the biggest captaincy crisis since Greg Chappell told his brother Trevor to bowl underarm.

As it turned out, that was underplaying it spectacularly.

'A knock on the door': How the sandpaper scandal kicked off

Reporter Chris Barrett revisits the nastiness, distrust and leaks behind Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa.

Newlands was the setting for Australian cricket to tip over the edge. The result was a reckoning for the national team, and the game.

Writing about it was an assignment like no other.

On my first night in South Africa, I was sipping a pint of Castle Lager at a hotel bar in Durban and heard that Australia wanted to have the stump microphones turned down when they were in the field.

The inference was obvious – the tourists didn’t want their on-field utterances towards the South Africans to be picked up by the viewing public as they tended to be when playing in the country, where the dial was usually kept up.

The request to Supersport, the South African network that televised the series and eventually zeroed in on Bancroft in Cape Town, was ignored.

Some in the Australian camp would later come to believe the broadcaster was weaponised against them in following the ball around as they fielded – to an ultimately devastating effect.

In Durban, Australia’s initial reaction to the stump microphones being left on was light-hearted. With some impromptu ambush marketing, they used the opportunity to promote Cricket Australia’s sponsors.

“How good is Qantas?” one player was heard saying to one of the umpires, whose sponsor was Emirates.

But it did not take long for an atmosphere of enmity to intensify, stirred up by alleged insults traded by Warner and de Kock.

The press pack was staying in the same hotel as the Australians, and I remember an annoyed Warner turning up in the breakfast room the morning after his run-in with de Kock.

Warner was not a bystander in proceedings, but he had been incensed by the gloveman’s alleged sledging about his wife Candice and strongly denied directing personal and family-related barbs of his own towards de Kock.

There was brief calm after we flew to Port Elizabeth for the second Test. The Australians brought with them a 1-0 lead, and Mitchell Marsh led morning dips in the surf opposite their luxury beachside lodgings.

But it did not take long for the hostility to ramp back up again. I just about fell off my chair in the press box at St George’s Park just after stumps one day when a source texted a photo of South African cricket officials posing with spectators wearing Sonny Bill Williams masks.

It took the heckling of Warner’s wife to a new level, who had many years earlier had a dalliance with the cross-code football star and was in the crowd with her and Warner’s two young daughters.

South African paceman Kagiso Rabada’s shoving of Australian captain Steve Smith after dismissing him had further flared tempers, and in a harbinger of things to come, distrust was also building about the two teams’ production of reverse swing – and how they were achieving it.

So much had gone on that by the time South Africa won in Port Elizabeth, levelling the series 1-1, the other Australian reporters and I took a collective breath as we paid a visit to the Addo Elephant National Park, thinking that the tour had surely hit its quota of nastiness and notoriety.

A nine-day break before the third Test in Cape Town put some distance between the rivals and offered those of us writing about them some downtime to explore the city and its surroundings.

We spent a few mornings climbing Table Mountain and Lion’s Head, visited Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela was once imprisoned, and joined team media manager Kate Hutchison and security manager Frank Dimasi for lunch at a winery in Stellenbosch.

I don’t know if Kate had access to a crystal ball, but as we gorged ourselves on a four-course meal and took in the view of the surrounding mountain ranges, she told us she had decided to move on from the often gruelling job after the tour.

When we got to Newlands, we sat down with Smith in a couple of rows of uncovered seating at the ground. He admitted he was tired after the Ashes in the previous Australian summer. He was also irritated by Rabada’s surprise exoneration for shoulder barging him, questioning why he wasn’t called as a witness to the appeal hearing, as well as a claim on South African bowler Vernon Philander’s social media account that he had taken a dive. Smith was not amused at Philander’s insistence that he had been hacked.

The Cape Town Test featured more abuse of players’ partners from beyond the boundary and a verbal run-in between Warner and a crowd member after he was bowled by Rabada in the first innings.

When I asked coach Darren Lehmann about the targeting of families in a press conference on the second evening, he called it “disgraceful”. It was a word that would be coined widely for what took place 40 minutes after lunch the next day.

This is burying the lede a little, but when the cheating storm blew up on the third afternoon at Newlands, I wasn’t there.

There is an unofficial rule imposed from sports desks that unless you’ve lost an arm you turn up at the ground, and I hadn’t missed a day’s play in the seven years I had been covering the Australian team.

My limbs were intact (as were those of colleagues who had swum with great white sharks in the gap between Tests), but on that day of days I was back at the hotel in the city centre, struck down by gastro and reporting on the match off the television.

Some of the Australian tour party had been isolated with the same illness, and we’d been asked not to show up if we caught it.

It was unfortunate timing for me, and I’ve never been thrilled about it, but there was a benefit to watching and listening to it all play out on the screen. As those who were sitting up late in Australia might remember, there was a build-up to the incident itself as the commentators made clear they suspected something was going on.

When it became obvious there was, I realised I would need to shake off the sickness and strap myself in for the rollercoaster that was to come.

It began with Smith and Bancroft’s infamous post-play press conference, which they had been advised not to attend, and the firestorm that erupted when Australia woke up.

The next morning I got myself across to the team’s nearby hotel, the Southern Sun Cullinan, to scope out what intelligence I could. I was also tasked with capturing a photo for the next day’s front page so, armed with my iPhone 6, I took one of an ashen-faced Smith walking to the team bus as the team made their way back to the ground.

The shell shocked Australians were bowled out for 107 to lose the Test, but I don’t remember a ball of it, with attention fixed entirely on the underhanded tactics of the day before, who was behind them and what would happen next.

In a frenzy of phone calls to contacts in South Africa and Australia, I recall a feeling of trepidation as I sent in a story the next day saying that Warner was being cast as the chief conspirator and he and Smith were facing bans, even though I was sure of the information.

That anxiety was nothing, though, compared to the panic coursing through me when I set off soon after for the final destination of the tour, Johannesburg, but was told at Cape Town airport that I had been placed on standby for my flight because it was overbooked.

Cricket Australia chief executive James Sutherland had flown into Johannesburg from Melbourne and was due to front a press conference at which it was thought he would announce sanctions against the players. I would miss it for sure if I had to wait for another plane.

As I fretted about being in the wrong place at the wrong time again, it emerged that Warner had been booted out of the team’s WhatsApp. After confirming that was right with a couple of phone calls, I sat on an unused old plastic chair in the terminal and frantically thrashed out an article.

Thankfully, there was a no-show or two at the airport, and after keeping an eye out for any late-arriving passengers running towards the check-in counter, I was relieved when the airline staff called me over to tell me I had a seat and I made it in time.

As it turned out, Sutherland didn’t reveal the suspensions imposed on Smith, Warner and Bancroft at his presser. That came a day later, landing with a thud via email from Cricket Australia.

The media contingent had by then taken up residency in the foyer of the team’s Johannesburg hotel and we looked on as Smith farewelled teammates and wheeled his suitcase out to a waiting vehicle. Warner was nowhere to be seen. He had slipped out more quietly to the airport with his family.

The story, of course, did not slow down with their departures.

There were suggestions the banned trio might take their cases to a hearing, and Warner’s representatives requested transcripts from the interviews conducted during the Cricket Australia investigation in Cape Town.

Then there was Smith’s heart-wrenching press conference on arrival in Sydney and Bancroft and Warner’s own emotional public mea culpas.

There was still another match to play, too, with a new captain, Tim Paine, and a new-look team and more tears to come.

Lehmann announced on the day before the fourth Test that he was quitting, then in surreal scenes the team trained to the strains of Australian classic songs at top volume around the cauldron that is the Wanderers ground. The fact that one of the tunes was Reckless, by Australian Crawl, did not go unnoticed.

The match itself, which South Africa won by 492 runs to win the series 3-1, was the kind of pummelling to be expected when the Australians’ minds were elsewhere.

The Australian team would pick themselves up – I was lucky enough to be at Edgbaston the following year to watch Smith lead them to victory with his remarkable twin hundreds in the first Ashes Test. Warner and Bancroft were also back in the team.

While they paid a heavy price for their mistakes, their careers went on. Smith is still in the team, has been captain again, and will be in the line-up against South Africa in Durban this week for Australia’s first Test in the country in eight years.

Even so, the events of South Africa in 2018 left a lasting impression for those three and everyone else involved.

In many ways, it was the series the spirit of cricket forgot.

Those of us who were there will certainly never forget it.

Australia Test squad: Pat Cummins (c), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Cooper Connolly, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Matthew Kuhnemann, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Michael Neser, Matthew Renshaw, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc, Beau Webster.

For years, dementia researchers had no answers, but now the word ‘breakthrough’ is on their lips

Sydney Morning Herald October 06, 2026

A blood test that can cheaply detect the disease. Promising new treatments. These developments are game changers.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

For 20 years, dementia researchers were stuck in a frustrating quagmire. Promising drug trials repeatedly collapsed. A practical diagnostic test remained elusive. Billions of dollars were spent – but nothing worked. Pharmaceutical companies began to pull out. And dementia surged to become Australia’s No.1 killer.

Now, however, that impasse has lifted. At clinics and labs around the world, staff are cautiously embracing a new word: “Breakthrough.”

The first two drugs to successfully modify Alzheimer’s disease, the most common form of dementia, were approved by Australia’s medicine regulator, the Therapeutic Goods Administration, last year. A blood test that can detect biomarkers up to 20 years before a patient’s first forgotten word with 92 per cent accuracy was approved two months ago.

These developments are game changers. The disease is “no longer universally described as untreatable”, according to the World Alzheimer Report 2026 released late last month, and we’re entering a period of “remarkable scientific momentum”.

That’s evident in a busy global pipeline of 158 drugs being tested in 192 trials, from new brain-penetrating agents to mRNA vaccines and repurposed medications, including weight loss jabs and erectile dysfunction drugs.

“It’s like an explosion in developments across the board,” said University of NSW Professor Kaarin Anstey, who sits on the World Health Organisation’s dementia panel.

“We are also becoming more aware of the risk factors. It’s a very exciting time.”

Associate Professor Emma Devenney, a neurologist, recalls being urged to reconsider entering the field of dementia when she started out because it was considered so futile.

“This is changing the trajectory, which we haven’t been able to do until now,” she said. “It’s lovely for patients and their families to have some hope.”

An estimated 460,000 Australians are living with dementia: a figure that’s forecast to blow out to half a million in the next three years and double to a million by 2061.

Our prevalence rate sits behind countries with older populations such as Japan, Germany and Italy. But the Asia-Pacific region has been singled out as a timebomb, with rates expected to triple in line with ageing populations and lifestyle factors by 2050 – at which point it will be home to half of the world’s cases.

This isn’t a foregone conclusion, though. New testing and treatments – combined with a growing body of evidence for prevention – aim to detect, and slow or stop dementia before symptoms appear.

Until now, the only way to get an accurate diagnosis for Alzheimer’s was to undergo a lumbar puncture or positron emission tomography (PET) scan, both of which are expensive, invasive and impossible to scale to meet demand.

An influx of new blood tests is set to simplify and democratise the process. Described as the “holy grail”, the newly approved pTau217 blood test is just as accurate as the two current gold standard tests but returns a result in minutes for a fraction of the cost, about $400. It isn’t yet subsidised.

Neuroscience Research Australia (NeuRA) chief executive Professor Matthew Kiernan said the test, which detects levels of abnormal tau proteins – a key biomarker for Alzheimer’s – empowers doctors and patients in determining treatment. It also accelerates research. “Eventually, it will be a test you can get at your local blood lab,” Kiernan said.

Similarly, until new drugs were approved last year, people living with Alzheimer’s disease had limited medical options. Medication could provide relief from symptoms, but there was nothing that would tackle the disease itself.

The new drugs are monoclonal antibodies, donanemab and lecanemab, which work by harnessing a recipients’ own immune system to break down sticky amyloid-beta plaques that accumulate around the brain and are known as hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease.

While they have each been proven to remove plaque and slow progression, they’ve also faced criticism for offering limited real-world benefits to only some patients at high cost and a risk of side effects, including swelling and bleeds in the brain.

“[Donanemab and lecanemab] work in that they are really good at removing amyloid in the brain, even if the clinical benefit isn’t as much as we would hope for,” Devenney said. “We’ve shown the approach can work. Hundreds of drugs haven’t worked.”

There’s clearly an appetite. Kiernan reports some patients are digging into their superannuation to fund the unsubsidised therapies, which can add up to $100,000 a year with medical fees and required brain scans.

“It’s turning the disease back,” he said. “The first [generation of drugs] are never the best, but they are starting the whole area of treatment.”

The next generation of monoclonal antibodies are designed to be more targeted with fewer side effects. They include trontinemab, which penetrates the blood-brain barrier more efficiently and works three times faster, according to early data. Its manufacturer calls this technology its “brainshuttle” delivery system.

“I think that’s going to be a real breakthrough,” Devenney said.

An international trial on 1600 middle-aged to older people with no memory problems but whom blood tests show are likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease in the future is under way. Like a “statin for the brain”, the hope is that trontinemab could prevent the disease from getting a foothold in the first place.

Former deputy principal Bill Yeates, from Sydney’s northern beaches, was blindsided by a young onset Alzheimer’s diagnosis at 59. He’d cared for his father through dementia years earlier and knew what lay ahead.

“It was devastating,” he said. “To be honest, I didn’t cope. I went into depression. It was really dark. I stayed at home, drank too much, and put on over 26 kilograms. I was concerned with losing my identity.”

Seven years later, it’s a different picture. The father-of-three changed his mindset, overhauled his lifestyle, enrolled in a clinical trial and established his own holistic approach to fight the disease.

“There are things I can invest in, things that I can choose to do, to show I am fighting this disease as best I can,” he said.

As well as a healthy diet, taking physical exercise, socialising, training his brain and ensuring he gets enough sleep, he secured extended access to an experimental drug XPro1595 that targets inflammation in the brain, another driver in Alzheimer’s.

“Good things were happening [on the drug] so I think I was one of the outliers,” he said. “Sadly, it failed, so I lost access in July 2025.”

A PET scan a year later showed the amount of amyloid-beta in his brain had increased significantly since his diagnosis, despite the fact he appeared to be functioning well. This was a blow – “I thought everything I’d done had been a waste of time” – until his doctor convinced him it wasn’t the whole picture.

A lot of research focuses on the “amyloid hypothesis”, in which the accumulation of plaque around brain cells is believed to be the underlying driver for Alzheimer’s disease. It makes sense: this process begins decades before symptoms appear and stabilises about 10 years before onset.

However, there’s another important hallmark: the tau protein that becomes abnormal and tangles into stringy clumps inside brain cells, leading to disrupted pathways and cell death. This process strongly correlates with the progression of symptoms.

Under the amyloid theory, stopping the plaque attack would prevent the disease from cascading into inflammation, tau tangles and cell death.

But given the complexity and differing pathways of dementia, it may not be that simple. Queensland Brain Institute researchers are working to develop new antibodies to clear tau tangles, while a gene-silencing drug called diranersen, which lowers the body’s production of tau, has recorded a 26 per cent slowing of decline in clinical trials.

Yeates is on the frontline: he learnt just two weeks ago that he had been accepted into a new trial of a promising monoclonal antibody called MK-2214 that targets abnormal tau. After that, he hopes to get in an amyloid-beta therapy trial.

“Even if it’s false, it gives me hope,” he said. “I think that’s the most important thing: having hope.”

His multi-targeted approach make sense: amyloid and tau therapies are being trialled simultaneously on patients in the long-running Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network (DIAN) trials.

“The reality is for people who are symptomatic, it probably will be a combination therapy [that is most effective],” said Devenney, who is NSW’s principal investigator for the international DIAN at NeuRA.

But penetrating the brain presents a significant challenge in treatment. The blood-brain barrier is notoriously difficult to cross, meaning large doses can be required to have an effect. This is why mRNA technology – which could leapfrog the barrier and send an instruction book to cells to direct your immune system to target specific proteins – is so appealing.

At The Florey in Melbourne, Associate Professor Rebecca Nisbet is working to develop Alzheimer’s vaccines with her team. They’re drawing on the city’s trove of mRNA technology, developed during the race for a COVID vaccine.

Nisbet acknowledges monoclonal antibodies are “a massive step forward” but hearing from people living with dementia who couldn’t access clinics nor afford treatment inspired her to seek out a more accessible option.

“[A vaccine] could cost as little as $50 a dose,” she said. “Ideally, we would be aiming for self-administration but it could also be done by a GP.”

A vaccine targeting amyloid-beta has progressed most quickly and is ready to go into the next phase of clinical development.

“We were able to show all mice that were vaccinated stimulated an immune response against amyloid peptides and had reduced amyloid build-up in the brain,” Nisbet said. Despite these promising results and potential cost benefits, she is less optimistic about the next phase of funding – a concern universally shared in the field.

Clinical trials are expensive and many pharmaceutical companies are reluctant to invest, particularly after a development drought and in an environment in which US President Donald Trump speaks unfavourably about vaccines. It’s a scenario grimly known as the “Valley of Death” between promising research and commercial viability. Exacerbating the financial stress, a string of medical development grants have recently been discontinued.

Vaccines for a condition such as Alzheimer’s may seem outlandish, but there’s already evidence they may have a role. Receiving the shingles vaccine has been shown to lower the risk of older people developing dementia by 29 per cent. Intriguingly, it seems to be about more than simply dodging the virus itself: the older version of the vaccine didn’t record the same benefit. An additive that is used to boost immune response may be the hero ingredient.

“There are components of the shingles vaccine that are protective against dementia, and it’s an exciting area to explore further,” Nisbet said.

In the meantime, Kiernan suggests the age at which Australians become eligible for a free dose of the vaccine should be lowered from 65 to 50 to secure benefits before significant brain changes occur.

“You’d get your vaccine, do your bowel test and a brain check at the age of 50,” he said. “That’s what we need to work towards as a community because our economy isn’t going to be able to sustain the cost [of dementia].”

Other vaccines – including flu, pneumococcal, RSV and diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis – are also associated with a lower risk of dementia.

Repurposed drugs – developed to treat one condition but which turn out to offer benefits for other conditions – may also be part of the puzzle in dementia, in the same way aspirin use extended from painkiller to prevention of heart attacks and blood clots.

It makes sense as it is unlikely that there will be one treatment for everyone: dementia is an umbrella term for various conditions that cause loss of cognitive function, including memory.

Others include vascular dementia and Lewy body dementias, which can cause hallucinations, delusions, paranoia and anxiety. Actor Bruce Willis is among those living with frontotemporal dementia, which targets the part of the brain involved in language and behaviour.

While most research centres on Alzheimer’s, it’s common for people to have more than one type of dementia. Devenney says work is being undertaken to tackle all forms of the disease.

“We do know what the pathology is with other types of dementia,” she said. “[One] approach is more broadly to look at the overlap, look at them together and also what’s different.”

The erectile dysfunction drug Viagra has been linked to a lower risk of vascular dementia in University of Oxford research, though more research is needed. There’s a plausible mechanism: it works by improving blood flow, which is impaired in this form of the disease.

Researchers are investigating whether Riluzole, a drug used to treat motor neurone disease, could improve cognition in people with Alzheimer’s and reduce build-up of amyloid in the brain.

Hope turned to disappointment for GLP-1 drugs as a potential treatment last year after large trials found they did not slow progression of early-stage Alzheimer’s. But the drugs, which include Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro, are linked to a lower risk of developing dementia among people taking them for diabetes and weight loss.

With the support of his wife, family and friends, Yeates is determined to “keep swimming” through good and bad days.

A Dementia Australia advocate, he presents at international conferences, champions the needs of people living with dementia and shares his story to reduce stigma.

“There might not be a cure,” he said. “But there can be a ray of hope that you can use to live a good life, doing the things you want to do.

“I’m optimistic for the future.”

Jeffrey Archer, former Conservative politician and novelist, dies aged 86

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 20:42:02 GMT

Lord Archer died peacefully at home between writing sessions, his publisher said

The author and former politician Jeffrey Archer has died aged 86.

Archer, who was a Conservative MP for five years before serving as the party’s deputy chairman, died peacefully at his home between writing sessions on Monday, his publisher Harper Collins said.

He had a successful career as a novelist and was made a life peer in 1992.

His political career was paused in 2001 with the disgrace of his being imprisoned for four years for perjury and perverting the course of justice.

An Old Bailey jury found that he had lied in a libel action he had brought against the Star newspaper 13 years earlier, in which he was awarded £500,000 damages.

He was released early in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.

London to Chicago BA flight declares emergency after dropping 28,000 feet

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 20:33:30 GMT

British Airways Boeing abruptly lost altitude over Ireland due to ‘technical issue’ and returned to Heathrow

A flight from London to Chicago declared an emergency after a sudden and steep descent of 28,000 feet over Ireland and was forced to turn back to Britain.

British Airways flight BA295 was bound for Chicago’s O’Hare airport but after a “technical issue” during which oxygen masks were deployed from the ceiling, the plane landed safely back at London Heathrow.

The aircraft, a Boeing 777-200ER, had departed Heathrow at 12.14pm on Monday for its scheduled transatlantic flight, and an hour into the journey had ascended to its cruising altitude of 37,000 feet.

According to passengers, the plane then encountered turbulence moments before the masks dropped, prompting “uncertainty” among those on board.

Pilots descended to below 10,000 feet and issued a 7700 emergency squawk to air traffic control – the international general emergency code – and made a U-turn to head back towards England.

Flight-tracking services showed the aircraft flying in a looping holding pattern over the Bristol Channel between Pembrokeshire and North Devon as the plane burnt off fuel in order to lower its weight, allowing the pilots to make a normal landing just after 5pm.

Passenger Tom Nicholls said there was a “sudden bit of turbulence” before the emergency was declared and that the quick descent to 9,000ft hadn’t been too uncomfortable.

He said: “The plane adjusted but it didn’t feel like it was descending rapidly. I’d say the pilots did a very good job.

“The oxygen masks popped out soon after and there was a bit of uncertainty onboard. The couple in front couldn’t get to theirs but by the time they’d found a spare seat with a mask, the captain announced we were below 10,000ft so they were not needed.”

A spokesperson for BA said: “The safety of our customers and crew is always our top priority, and the aircraft landed safely after our highly trained pilots returned to Heathrow following a technical issue.

“Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible.”

Photographs taken by passengers and shared on social media showed oxygen masks dangling from the ceiling as the plane made the return journey.

A rapid descent to below 10,000 feet and a 7700 emergency squawk are routinely associated with aircraft experiencing cabin depressurisation but the official cause of the emergency has yet to be confirmed by BA.

The Boeing 777-200ER is one of BA’s oldest planes in service, having been delivered to the carrier almost 30 years ago – in July 1997. Live streams showed the aircraft making its descent and safe landing back to Heathrow.

Many passengers have been booked on to new flights departing on Tuesday.

How do sports fans end up as aggressive defenders of a nation state’s regime?

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 20:08:05 GMT

The Manchester City case is one example of how fandom has warped beyond previous boundaries in online spaces

A video of Liam Gallagher playing in a 1996 charity football match resurfaced on social media recently. Dressed in Manchester City blue and a bucket hat, in truth he appears to be in a fug of cigarettes and alcohol. But then, out of nowhere, he hits a shot into the top corner. Since last week, though, the Oasis singer has preferred to defend the honour of his club with his studs up.

As the fallout from the biggest scandal in British football history headed into a second week, Gallagher was asked what he made of rival fans wanting City to lose all their trophies after being found guilty of all the serious charges against them. “There all NEUROTIC little GIMPS,” came the reply on social media. It was one of dozens of sweary, punchy, and often amusing responses, all built on a solitary article of faith: that City will somehow find a way to wriggle free.

But Gallagher is hardly standing alone. Over at Bluemoon, the biggest City forum, the tone has been just as defiant – albeit with a sprinkle of gallows humour. “Have we been blamed for the Titanic hitting the iceberg yet?” asked one user. “Manchester City shot JFK,” wrote another. “This isn’t just a fight between the PL & City. It’s a fight for the heart, soul & future of football,” reckoned a third.

Staggeringly, the forum now has over 192,000 posts since the initial charges against City, dating back to 2023. Naturally the Premier League, jealous rivals and the media all come under heavy fire. Yet there remains a curious reluctance among fans to accept wrongdoing – or to criticise the club’s owners.

How might we explain that? I am not sure it is down to pure tribalism, or a determination among City fans to wait for the club’s appeal to play out. It’s more complicated, and more interesting, than that.

Let us try to get into the head of the most vociferous City fan since last Tuesday. For decades they were in United’s shadow, then everything changed. Their city did too, given how much Abu Dhabi United Group pumped into it. You can forgive them, then, for not wanting to believe that it was all built on sand during the legal process.

But now? Now there is no excuse. So what might explain the reluctance to accept what the independent commission report lays out in great detail? According to the Irish academic Colm Kearns, one reason is because the United Arab Emirates has not only brought unprecedented success and forged emotional bonds with City fans “but have also co-opted elements of the club’s fanbase as aggressive defenders of their regime”.

In 2023 Kearns and his colleagues analysed huge numbers of posts from City fans, going back years, and found that some of them would not only “overlook ethical violations by the Group, but decry and – in some cases – attack the Group’s critics.”

In other words the club’s owners had successfully leveraged the tribal loyalty of City fans into being Manchurian Candidates – or, rather, Manchesterism Candidates.

Kearns tells me that some sports journalists had even self-censored because of the impact of online abuse from City fans. “We had people talking about how fans would go online and try to find their troll through their personal social feeds, and it sent that on to their editor to get them in trouble,” he says.

There is another massive factor here: social media, and the way we now consume sport and communicate with other fans. Thirty years ago, most City fans would live near Manchester and see fans from other clubs at work and in the pub. Nowadays, they can dwell in an online space made up entirely of people who support their own club.

“I think it makes fans perhaps more tribally myopic than they would have been before and less likely to look outside of their own club’s perspective,” says Kearns.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Academics also talk of “sports fandom circles”, in which supporters across the globe increasingly mobilise and fiercely defend athletes or their teams. That phenomenon, which came out of east Asia with popular culture and music, leads supporters to be laser-focused on their own tribe. But it hardly encourages lighthearted banter, common ground, or compromise.

In City’s case, Kearns suspects that some fans are putting the club above the wider game, citing a Reddit post that said: “I am a City fan first and a football fan second.” Although, as he concedes, it is impossible to know how many online posters do not live in Manchester, or go to games, and therefore feel the need to prove their bona fide credentials by sticking up for the club at all costs.

Either way, where we could go next is interesting. If you were a far-right tech billionaire, why wouldn’t you want to buy a successful sports team – especially if you knew there was an army of potential defenders of your reputation among your new fanbase?

Over the weekend I went through the fan forums of other clubs to see what their supporters made of the guilty verdict against City. The overwhelming majority welcomed it, of course, even if some questioned whether City would really get properly punished for their crimes, given the relationship with Abu Dhabi and the British government.

“Once you lose faith that the rules apply equally, football becomes something else,” one wrote. “Every title, every match, carries a question mark. I feel cheated. I’m one of the victims. And for that, I hate Manchester City.”

Some will agree with that sentiment. Others will raise their eyebrows. I do wonder, though, would that poster feel the same way if the boot was on the other foot, and their club was in the line of fire?

Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 20:06:18 GMT

Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surge

Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.

The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.

“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.”

Speaking outside the White House on Monday, Donald Trump told reporters: “Well, it’s a big victory: close but a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually.”

Trump, who is a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, predicted the runoff would be “a very close election”.

The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro.

The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.

Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.

Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.

Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.

Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.

“We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.

Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said.

Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.

“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”

The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.

The result is good news for Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, and his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.

One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.

The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”

Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.

But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.

Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.

Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.

Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”.

Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups,” Rocha added.

Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

Saudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in Yemen

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 19:44:01 GMT

Government offensive launched under air cover by Saudi military coalition aims to retake all Houthi-held territory

Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several key areas around Bab al-Mandab strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said on Monday.

The officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government have retaken the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait. They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns.

The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under an air cover by a Saudi military coalition, aiming to retake all territory held by the Houthis.

However, the offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the south-western part of Yemen, taking the key town of Turbah in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward the strategic provincial capital of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.

The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis. He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign.

Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government in Yemen would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, the US secretary of state said that Saudi Arabia and the US had a defense agreement but would not offer more details.

He said the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis had come under attack, and “they have a right to defend themselves”.

The new push sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.

The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.

The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.

“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.

Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.

Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.

Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.

Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.

A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at the Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in the Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.

The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.

There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.

Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
