Republicans criticize Steve Hilton for ‘creepy’ innuendo-filled campaign ad

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 19:28:42 GMT

Hilton faces heavy backlash from within his own party for ‘Just Try It’ ad amid his longshot bid for California governor

Steve Hilton, the Republican candidate for California governor, is receiving heavy criticism from members of his own party over a controversial, sexual innuendo-filled campaign ad that has been described as “creepy”.

The video entitled “Just Try It, California” was released last week and depicts two young women with brightly colored hair, sitting on a bed in front of a pride flag in low lighting. One nervously says “I can’t believe I’m doing this”, while another strokes her hair and coaxes “don’t be nervous, it’s not that bad” before guiding her to fill out a ballot for Hilton and aggressively commanding “lick it”.

The controversy comes as Hilton, a British former political adviser to David Cameron and Fox News host, is fighting to advance his longshot bid against Xavier Becerra, the former health secretary. With just a few weeks to go before the November midterms elections, Hilton is trailing in the polls.

Sonja Shaw, the Republican nominee for California superintendent of public instruction, called the new campaign ad “creepy, weird, disturbing garbage”.

“This is a clear example of exactly why good people are walking away from the Republican party. As a mother and someone who has fought to protect the innocence of children, this crosses a line. We have lost our way,” she wrote on social media.

Michael Gates, the party’s nominee for state attorney general, also condemned the advertisement, stating that he “emphatically [denounced] the use of young women as a political tool”.

Hilton faces tough odds in the deep blue state, where voters haven’t elected a Republican to lead since 2004. Polls have consistently shown Becerra with a significant lead over Hilton.

Hilton is trying to rally California’s Republicans while converting Democrats and independents frustrated with the ever-increasing cost of living in California.

In a video posted shortly after the ad was launched, Hilton said it had largely been positively received but that he recognized that people were offended, and that was not his campaign’s intention.

“We were trying to make a point in a provocative way, in satirical way,” he said. “It grieves me that you’ve been upset by this. But I also want to ask you to understand what we are doing, why we’re doing it and to ask for some grace as well as understanding as we fight this campaign.”

Becerra was quick to jump on the controversy, posting an article about his own support for Medicare for All with a line directed at his rival: “Steve, just try it!”

Green party of England and Wales facing international ostracism over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 19:10:43 GMT

European Green party says motion goes against its policy, with German Green co-leader calling it ‘intolerable and unacceptable’

Zack Polanski may rue lack of leadership when Greens needed him to act

The English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after adopting a policy declaring Zionism as a form of racism, which has drawn dismay from the group representing European Greens.

The co-leader of the German Greens separately said the policy was “intolerable and unacceptable”, running contrary to its belief in the right of Israel to exist.

The binding policy motion passed in a vote at the Greens’ conference in Brighton on Sunday. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed it.

The policy says Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, should be “treated as any other form of racism”, and backs a single democratic Palestinian state across historic Palestine “with equal rights for all”.

The European Green party, which represents 47 parties, including the Green party of England and Wales (GPEW), said it supported a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, and the new motion went against this.

The alliance “will immediately demand clarity from the leadership and parliamentary group of GPEW, to understand the official party policy of GPEW, how they position themselves towards the self-determination of Israelis and Jews as well as the protection of Jewish people and members in the party”, it said in a statement.

Felix Banaszak, the leader of the German Greens, known formally as Alliance 90/the Greens, told a press conference the motion was “intolerable and unacceptable”.

“It runs counter to everything that Alliance 90/the Greens stands for in Germany, and it also runs counter to what the European Green party stands for,” he added.

Banaszak said: “There is a widely held view within the European Green party that Israel has a right to exist and that this right must not be undermined.” His party would “approach our partner parties in Europe to clarify how to deal with this”.

Sandy Ruthven, the chair of Amnesty International UK’s charitable trust and a longstanding Green member, resigned over the motion and accused the party of failing to confront antisemitism.

The fallout from Sunday’s vote has also intensified a debate over whether the Greens’ highly decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly.

Policy is made at the party’s two annual conferences, which generally involve a small proportion of members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership.

Ellie Chowns, a former co-leader, said the party’s governance and policymaking “urgently need to be modernised”.

“As a party we pride ourselves on our democratic member-led policymaking process, but I do think we need to ask ourselves some searching questions when less than 1% of our members actually participate,” Chowns, the Green MP for North Herefordshire, told the Guardian. “This is long overdue and has become even more urgent with the huge expansion of our membership.”

Chowns said she understood the concerns of European Greens, which she shared, but stressed: “There is still much more that unites us than divides us.”

One source in the party said the criticism from European Greens, especially those in Germany, was understandable given their differing stances on Gaza and Israel.

They said: “The German Greens support arming Israel, opposed a ceasefire to Israel’s onslaught on Gaza, backed the suspension of funding to Unrwa and co-sponsored a Bundestag resolution describing the arguments and methods of the peaceful, Palestinian-led BDS campaign as antisemitic.”

Any change to internal party structures would be hard to implement. One Green insider said that to give MPs greater authority over members would undermine the party’s commitment to grassroots democracy. However, they said the existing model could produce a lack of coherence and strategic direction, while giving a disproportionate influence to members with the most time to participate in policymaking.

They suggested members could determine broad strategic priorities, with smaller bodies developing detailed policy while remaining accountable to the membership.

Another senior Green defended the party’s model of direct democracy, arguing that allowing members to determine policy was fundamental to the party’s character.

Daniel Schuster, the regional director of the Simon Wiesenthal Center’s European office, said: “The British Green party’s decision to formally classify Zionism as a form of racism is absurd, not based on any logical basis and is itself racist. And timing, just days before the third anniversary of the 7 October terrorist Hamas attacks, is designed to inflict pain on a deeply solemn occasion.

“Branding Zionism itself as racism crosses a profoundly consequential line. It takes a movement for Jewish national self-determination and transforms it into something for which Jews are expected to apologise. We will not.”

In a statement, the Green party leader in England and Wales, Zack Polanski, said: “Antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct – blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe. It’s our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK. As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of.”

He added: “Through the Green party’s unified stance and dedicated pressure, we have begun to shift this government away from its complicity with the Israeli government’s atrocities in Gaza, with the foreign secretary now taking the long overdue step of ending trade with illegal settlements.”

Other party insiders – possibly more plugged into what is going on in their constituencies – concede that Farage still represents a huge threat. They are among those concerned about Badenoch pitching to the right.

Instead, they say that she needs to do more to win over centrist voters for the party to stand a chance of winning another election. Part of that is by focusing more on the economy and less on culture wars.

Badenoch believes she can “shrug off” the Liz Truss anchor and beat Reform and Labour on the economy, MPs say. Andrew Griffith, her shadow chancellor who has previously worked in business, helps the party’s credibility, they add, and Badenoch will speak more about the topic this week.

The Tory leader also polls ahead of her party, which insulates her from much internal criticism. One adviser said the Tories do better when their leader is in that position – citing David Cameron and Boris Johnson – but worse when they’re behind, as Rishi Sunak was.

Badenoch has told her top team that they have to work “day by day” to restore the party’s fortunes. Yet there is no escaping that almost two years after she was elected as leader, the Tories are still polling lower than they did in 2024 with their catastrophic general election defeat.

“You won’t hear much from us on that,” one senior aide said. “The qualitative stuff is good but it’s not backed up yet by the numbers. We need to put on three or four points in the polls. If we do that and gain momentum we’re back.”

Others are hopeful that the exposure of their conference week can give them enough of a lift in the polls to help them maintain the narrative that they’re on the march.

The spectre hanging over the whole affair, however, is the prospect of a snap general election. Andy Burnham’s political away day at Chequers on Monday has got many Tories spooked, even though the prime minister has ruled out calling an early election.

Perhaps more in hope than expectation, shadow cabinet ministers said they did not believe Burnham would call an election. “He said it would be irresponsible and it’s hard to walk that back,” said one.

However, Badenoch told a bash for Tory MPs on Sunday night the party was getting ready for an election regardless. But while she sounded bullish, her closest lieutenants are anything but. “If there is one, we’re all fucked,” they said.

Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers from the Gloucestershire base over security concerns about a possible threat from Iran.

The prime minister’s spokesperson, speaking during a scheduled briefing, said “yes” when asked if the military site was safe – contrasting with the concern the US military revealed during the hasty redeployment the day before.

Pointing to comments made last week by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the official said there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”.

Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that the Pentagon confirmed on Sunday evening.

US officials told the New York Times commanders had received new information about an Iran-backed plot against the base, which has been on high alert for more than a week. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US.

Donald Trump said on Monday that the United States had withdrawn the bombers from the base because of “some threats”, without saying what they were.

“There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” Trump said.

UK sources said they were not aware of a new terrorism threat to the base and that they would be surprised if Iran had the capability to orchestrate a fresh threat, a week after five men from London were arrested late at night having driven to a village near the base in white vans with an unclear purpose.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Monday that the redeployment of the bombers was not tied to the arrests and tried to downplay any discrepancies with the UK. He said the US was confident in the security of all its bases and “with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely for a long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative”.

Downing Street’s comments were the first made by the UK in the light of the US withdrawal. Neither the Ministry of Defence nor Gloucestershire police commented when asked if there was any additional threat to residents near the base. Other UK officials indicated they had not been briefed on US thinking.

RAF Fairford has already been on high alert for several weeks amid heightened US concern that Tehran could try to instigate an attack on the base, which was used for US air force bombing runs against Iran earlier this year. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that the base was a legitimate military target.

The hasty redeployment arguably represents a victory for Iran, forcing US bombers to retreat without any kind of attack taking place, though some experts said Washington was engaging in a wider redeployment that could lead to a scaling up of operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in November.

It is unclear what level of threat Tehran could pose to a base in the heart of the UK, though Iran has destroyed US planes on the tarmac during fighting this year. Missiles fired from Iran may be able to reach the UK but would be likely to be shot down first, and a drone attack would be a high-risk operation close to the base.

Experts said the size of the airbase meant it was difficult to protect it from a short-range drone attack, perhaps similar to the attempt to bomb Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig airport in Germany in August, which the country’s authorities attributed to Russia.

But there was caution that there remained a lack of information. “Airfields are hard to defend, but the US could be making a point or just being very cautious,” said Matthew Savill, an expert with the Royal United Services Institute.

Developments in the UK have not so far matched the apparent level of US concern. The five men from London were arrested in Whelford, next to the base, on suspicion of carrying explosives, but they were not charged.

No explosive devices were found in the search of the vans or the men, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. All five were released on bail a day later.

Trump said afterwards that he was surprised they had been allowed out on bail. “We know everything about them, we would not have released them,” he said.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been more muted. He said last week that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, but developments in the British investigation, led by counter-terrorism police, have been limited.

A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing acts of terrorism, but he was also released on bail on Saturday. Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the events in Gloucestershire were continuing, counter-terrorism police said.

Speaking at a Centre for Policy Studies meeting in Birmingham, Stephenson claimed to know Luton well because he lives in a neighbouring constituency. “I know Luton reasonably well because I live 10, 15 minutes away and represent Mid Bedfordshire, I live in a village just over the border.

“You know, equality should be equality for all. It’s a fairly, fairly simple concept, but it’s actually become quite a complicated construct. And the people that are losing out are white young men,” he said.

He claimed that some government schemes did not allow young white men to apply. “I’m not surprised that young white men feel like the system is rigged against them, particularly with the government coming out with schemes that won’t allow them to apply for internships. Jude awakening: how a more fluid England are ‘unlocking’ Bellingham’s full potential

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 18:00:49 GMT

Anthony Barry knows the hunt is on. The England assistant coach has been through the debriefs. He has mulled over the minutiae with Thomas Tuchel to such an extent he is allowed to make a joke at the boss’s expense. “He’s doing my head in,” Barry says with a smile. What is the missing piece of the puzzle? After all the emotion of England’s semi-final finish at the World Cup, how can they take the decisive step to glory?

It is early days in the Nations League campaign, which everybody at the Football Association wants to use as a slingshot into Euro 2028 when England will co-host, but Barry can see the genesis of an answer. It comes down to liberation, enabling England’s top players to fully express themselves, and there is a reason why he finds himself talking about Jude Bellingham.

The Real Madrid player was sensational in Saturday’s 7-0 win over Croatia in Rijeka, just as he was in the 3-2 defeat against Spain at Wembley on the Saturday before that. Playing in the No 10 role but with greater licence to drift, to overload on either side, there were times when Bellingham seemed to be playing with his own ball.

The story about why he wore the No 22 shirt at his first club, Birmingham, is well told. Because he was a No 4, a No 8 and a No 10 rolled into one. Tuchel appears to have reached a conclusion, the basis of which was formed at the World Cup when Bellingham excelled: when a talent like him can play in so many positions, perhaps it is better not to give him one at all.

“The structure [now in the Nations League] allows Jude to play more from his intuition,” Barry says, “and less from being locked down or caged in a certain position. It allows him to roam and operate in spaces in which he thinks he can be dangerous and so far it’s brought out the best in him.

“It is a challenge because Jude can play in any of those positions comfortably and on a high level. So the challenge is to give him a space where he can do it all at once inside of one game. Right now, in a short sample, it seems like we found a solution to unlock all of the potential that Jude has. But we have to continue.”

The point is that it is not just about Bellingham, even if he has drawn the eye almost inexorably so far this season. The blueprint was there for all to see against Croatia and it is one in which plenty of players were encouraged to push into new zones away from those traditionally dictated by their positions. Hence Tuchel had the full-backs extremely high, the wingers making zipping runs off the sides.

It is about the combinations, the slicker the better, but also about players dropping into unusual areas to provide cover and using their footballing intelligence to ensure the overall structure retains its shape. Hence there was the sight of Harry Kane dropping into defensive spaces out of possession, the kind where most No 9s would never tread.

It was impossible to ignore the ferocity of England’s counterpress; how if one player lost the ball, he and his teammates sought to regain it within two or three seconds. Croatia were overwhelmed, especially in the first half, which ended with England four goals up. The intensity has to endure. But it is the proactive add-ons that the management hope will drive the new tournament cycle, continuing against Czechia in the Nations League at Wembley on Tuesday night. It is no longer a positional style. The idea is that it is freer. Is it a reaction to the inhibitions England came to feel in the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina?

“We have moved to a more principle-driven approach, which allows for more flexibility and fluidity,” Barry says. “But fluidity only looks good if it’s anchored by real principles. There is always a danger in international football with such a lack of time to prepare that if you go for this fluid model it can look quite messy. With the IQ of the players we have, it’s been quite natural for them to work together, operate in different spaces.

“It’s not about starting new, it’s about continuation and adding stuff on top. It’s less prescribed, less fixed in the idea of: ‘You play here, you play there.’ It’s more interchanges of position. We feel it suits this group of players and is the best way to break down opposing blocks.

The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.

This could mean as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state of Israel.

The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright.

Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and to impose sanctions on British firms that aid, support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements.

The Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, has said that Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country.

The consulate, which Israel’s foreign ministry has said will close on Thursday, is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza. It is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East ​Jerusalem.

An Israeli diplomatic source said: “There is no reason for us to respond to speculation about decisions that other countries may or may not take in the future.

“We have already demonstrated that any step taken against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and that will continue to be the case.”

The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Jerusalem last week in an effort to persuade the Israeli government to rescind or defer the closure of the consulate but the talks failed.

It has been reported that Powell opposed the decision of the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, to press ahead with the settlement trade ban decision, fearing that it might play to the advantage of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, in the national election on 27 October as he seeks to bolster his case that only his brand of leadership can bring Israel security. There is no evidence yet that the UK decision has featured in the campaign, but tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats may raise its profile.

The ‌incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.

Diplomats from other western countries have been very worried about the closure setting a precedent, and suggest that Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it has implications beyond the immediate dispute.

Shutting down the consulate involves Israel claiming authority in Jerusalem that it does not have under international law, so it is effectively a challenge to the status quo.

The Guardian view on Tory economics: Britain’s future needs more than Thatcher’s past

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 17:46:10 GMT

The Conservatives blame their failures on abandoning their 1976 principles. But the country needs investment and resilience rather than another round of spending cuts

The Conservative party wants to go back to the future under Kemi Badenoch. In her foundational text, The Right Way, released at the weekend, the Tory party leader makes its intellectual lineage explicit, repeatedly invoking Margaret Thatcher’s 1976 policy statement The Right Approach. The 2026 economic framework is familiar: only private enterprise creates wealth; taxes, regulation and spending can obstruct growth and competition; markets make the country stronger. The speech by her shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, made it clear that Conservative failures over its 14-year spell in charge were the result of the party straying from Thatcherite principles.

One might argue that, on the contrary, errors were because the party slavishly followed such a creed. When Rough, a depleted North Sea gasfield that once provided around 70% of the UK’s gas-storage capacity, was judged uneconomic by its private owner, a Conservative government in 2017 accepted that international markets could provide the UK with adequate energy security. That proved to be a big mistake when Russia invaded Ukraine, sending fossil fuel prices upwards. Britain was particularly exposed as a net energy importer and highly dependent on gas. Tory ministers had to bring back Rough into operation in 2022. Mrs Badenoch puts its closure down to “false economies”. But what was wrong was putting private profitability ahead of the country’s needs.

In his speech to conference, Mr Griffith attempted to distance himself and his party from the chaotic Liz Truss administration, although he was a member of its disastrous Treasury team. But his diagnosis today appears similar. Britain, in his telling, is supposedly more of a command economy than a market‑based one. To kickstart it, he argued, will require lower taxes, welfare reform and deregulation.

The difference, Mr Griffith was keen to stress, is that tax cuts will now come through spending cuts rather than additional borrowing. Why shrinking the state would strengthen growth enough to offset its effect on demand and productive capacity is unanswered. Just how big those cuts might be was revealed by the Guardian. Mr Griffiths admitted when he was the shadow business secretary that the Tories were planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the £47bn that the party had announced if it won the next election.

This might be seen as the kind of clear blue water that the Tories need to put between themselves and Labour. But the real enemy is further right. As the pollster John Curtice told a Demos fringe event, the voters most dissatisfied with high rates of immigration, the performance of the economy and the NHS are disproportionately moving to Reform UK. The perceived failures of Labour are not automatically benefiting the Conservatives. Prof Curtice said that either the party was “still getting the blame” for its record in government, or Reform was “simply speaking a language” that appeals more to those voters. It is hard to see how restoring Thatcherite principles will help the party here.

Mrs Badenoch recognises that the world has changed. She acknowledges that insecure supply chains and economic coercion may require the state to step in. But public investment must remain a special case, and, she says, “help to an individual firm should be exceptional and, where possible, temporary”. The real problem with her prospectus is Britain’s future requiring permission from 1976.

The Guardian view on sexual abuse in schools: teachers cannot deal with this alone

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 17:45:41 GMT

Politicians must redouble their efforts to tackle a disturbing pattern of pupils assaulting classmates

The Guardian’s findings about the extent of sexual abuse in schools require an urgent, calibrated response. Data revealing multiple rapes committed each year on school premises in England and Wales is hard to comprehend. Yet this is what freedom of information requests to police forces, covering the period from 2021 until last year, have revealed. As well as the severity of the offences, the youth of many of the victims is disturbing. More than 8,500 sexual offences at or near schools were committed against under-13s, most of them girls.

Data about perpetrators contains gaps, including their age and sex. While the overwhelming majority of such acts are carried out by boys, we don’t know the exact proportion, nor if there is an age gap between those carrying out abuse and those being targeted. Only 33 out of 43 police forces shared their data, meaning that large areas including Scotland are not represented. But whatever the exact details, and allowing for the fact that these are reports, not convictions, the findings are deeply dismaying.

The suggestion by the acting chief constable Becky Riggs, who leads on child protection and abuse investigation for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, that the figures could reflect an increased willingness to report sexual abuse rather than more abuse taking place, must be taken seriously. At the same time, an unknown number of assaults continue to go unreported. Exact comparisons with the past are not possible since there is no equivalent dataset. What can be said, 10 years after a committee of MPs recommended that ministers should make sexual abuse in schools an “immediate policy priority”, is that the problem has not gone away; some experts believe that it is getting worse.

The response to the problem so far has relied on three main tools. One is the promotion of sex and relationships education. The scale of image-based abuse in schools requires further investigation, but Monday’s warning of a huge rise in AI child sexual abuse material globally points to the need for a curriculum that keeps abreast of technological change. The second tool is online safety laws including age verification, tighter restrictions on pornography, and the pledge by Sir Keir Starmer’s government to place smartphones off-limits for under-16s. The third is the criminal justice system, and ongoing efforts to improve the way that police and prosecutors deal with victims.

Ministers will need all these to work if they are to have any chance of meeting their goal of halving violence against women and girls. But acute resource and capacity problems are hampering courts and prisons, while pornography regulation needs to be enforced as well as discussed. While campaigners are hopeful, effects need to be measured. In relationships education, good intentions must not be confused with effects. To make a difference, schools need investment, training and evaluation.

This problem cannot be left to teachers to deal with; parents should also discuss these issues with young people. And politicians will have to be brave. The focus on sexual crimes by rightwing and far-right parties in many countries places liberals in a difficult position, with some fearful that by talking about them, they risk adding to a narrative that sows discord and scapegoats immigrants. The abuse of children by other children is an upsetting subject, but looking away is the worst of all options. As a society, we owe it to young people to deal with it.

The FDF said 16 club presidents then entered the building under police escort and proceeded to hold what it described as a “purported” EGM. The federation rejected the meeting as illegitimate, saying it had not been properly convened and that the notice periods and procedures required under its statutes and electoral code had not been respected. It declared any decisions taken “null and void”. But sources in Djibouti have insisted the number of delegates required by the statutes was present. They unanimously voted to remove Waberi and the executive committee before establishing an interim committee to oversee the federation.

The confrontation follows weeks of mounting opposition to Waberi, a member of the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee as well as Fifa’s council and a close ally of Gianni Infantino. At the start of September, a coalition of 27 clubs announced its intention to vote on the removal of the executive committee and insisted it had secured the two-thirds support required under the federation’s statutes.

The FDF disputed that calculation, saying it has 67 members and that 45 – not 27 – would be required to trigger an extraordinary assembly. The dispute escalated as additional clubs and delegates joined the campaign against the executive committee. The government then intervened, with the secretary of state for sport, Fatouma Ali Abdallah, ordering the FDF to convene an extraordinary general assembly within 72 hours.

The FDF has appealed to Fifa and Caf, arguing that the use of state security forces to remove elected officials could constitute interference in the affairs of a national football association. It warned that the consequences could include suspension, exclusion of Djiboutian clubs and national teams from international competitions, and a freeze on development programmes and funding. The Guardian has requested a comment from Fifa.

It is understood Waberi and several other officials could be facing charges this week after a police investigation of the FDF related to suspected embezzlement and money laundering was completed. They were arrested in September 2024 after a government inspection of the FDF identified financial and administrative irregularities, including weaknesses in procurement, cash management and financial controls. The government’s investigation also raised concerns about anomalies in payments to third parties, failure to pay tax on salaries and wages and “misuse of cash payments” totalling almost £500,000. The police then carried out its investigation.

Waberi has denied wrongdoing. He said in August after the FDF was accused by a club official of misusing funds that Fifa’s “monitoring mechanisms have revealed no indication of wrongdoing regarding the funds it disbursed”.

No queues, empty seats and the worst speech ever heard: welcome to the Tory conference

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 17:34:45 GMT

Birmingham event is like a safari park attraction where we get to see the remnants of a party in a protected habitat

At the Labour party conference in Liverpool last week, Andy Burnham floated the idea of electoral reform. This week in Birmingham, the Tories have come up with a plan of their own: voting with their feet.

How to put this nicely? Let’s just say that the Conservative party conference is extremely civilised. No queues for the food concessions. No queues to get into any of the halls. In fact, the organisers are delighted that anyone has turned up at all.

This doesn’t feel like a high-octane meeting of a party preparing for government. More like a home counties meeting of the Rotary Club. On current evidence, if there is a general election next year – as Kemi Badenoch is trying to convince us there will be – then the Tories won’t be active participants. More like vaguely disinterested observers. For these four days, Birmingham is a city where you can sit and watch the world pass you by.

Not that those who have turned up seem unhappy. Rather, they are thrilled to find themselves still alive. This time last year, there was a possibility that they faced extinction: under threat from left and right and with a leader in Kemi who looked unlikely to last six months. Since then things have stabilised as Robert Jenrick has been stopped from pulling out their ventilator in the intensive care unit. They are now merely an endangered species. The conference centre is a safari park attraction where we get to see the remnants of the Tory party in a protected habitat.

The morning’s activities take place in what is optimistically called the main hall: a hard-to-find side room with a capacity of about 200. These are way more seats than any of the acts require. First up was shadow transport secretary, Richard Holden, who managed to bore even himself. Still, at least the hall was about a third full. Which, for Rich, is a major result. I’m guessing most of the people there were family and friends.

It was no fuller for the shadow health secretary, Damian Hinds, who stumbled over his notes for five minutes. Weirdly, there were 24 people watching an empty stage online after he had left, while only 17 had been online when he was talking. Or maybe that’s not so weird.

For the afternoon offering we were moved to a slightly bigger hall. This could have been a mistake. It had come billed as a “major speech by the shadow chancellor”. Only we were made to sit through an hour and a half of nothingness – an opportunity to deliberate our own and the Tories’ existential futility – before the main event.

By now at least another third of the audience had left. A wise choice. They clearly had some idea of what was coming. Even 20 minutes of Andrew Griffith can rip your soul in half. If only I had joined them.

Not that the hall was anywhere near full to begin with. First up was the shadow Defra secretary, Victoria Atkins, who had sensibly worked out that no one in their right mind would stay to hear her talk. So instead she positioned herself as a cable TV presenter – there were 53 people watching online – chatting to her guest, Jeremy Clarkson.

This did at least lift the mood in the hall. A genuine celeb was among them for 15 minutes. However, it doesn’t say much for your conference when your most popular speaker is someone who openly says he’s not a Tory party member and has only turned up because he will go anywhere people will have him to talk about farming.

“Wow,” said Jezza. “There’s an awful lot of people here dressed as seats!” Vicky giggled nervously. The rest of the chat came and went perfectly amiably. Jezza did what he does best, giving his best impression of a multimillionaire held back by the incompetence of government. Still, at least he injected some fun. Vicky wanted to know how the farming summer had gone. He replied that the Diddly Squat farm had produced several ounces of hen food because of the extreme heat.

Someone should have told him that Griffith was about to get rid of the Climate Change Committee. If you missed any of this, you will be able to watch extended highlights on the next series of Clarkson’s Farm.

From then on, the conference became one long car crash. A panel with a couple of rightwing hacks droning on about nothing and then another panel in which one businesswoman congratulated herself on not getting stabbed on the train to Brum – apparently all her friends refuse to use trains – and then a businessman sobbing at the thought of billionaires being asked to pay inheritance tax. Some of them are so sick with worry they can no longer sleep.

Finally the main attraction. What would turn out to be a landmark occasion for all party conferences. Because Griffith proceeded to give the worst speech ever heard. Not just in content but in delivery. It was like watching a less sentient version of the PG Tips monkey. Constantly applauding himself and ending his sentences with “Yeah”. What was left of the audience didn’t know where to look.

If Andy really is the future chancellor, then we are truly fucked. Even Mel Stride wasn’t this hopeless. We might as well all pack up now. He was going to build more homes that were uninsulated and might fall down because they were cheaper. He would cut taxes and regulations the Tories had themselves introduced.

“This is our destiny,” he said. And then he dematerialised. It was as though he had been primitive AI and his controller had seen quite enough and decommissioned him. Andy didn’t know he had finished. And neither did anyone else.

Daryz’s Arc reputation secure but retirement would rule out folk-hero status

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 17:24:35 GMT

Back-to-back wins is a huge achievement, but owners have more to think about than unprecedented third title

It was, as the moderator of the post-Arc press conference put it, the “difficult question everyone wants to ask”, but Princess Zahra Aga Khan, the owner of the winner, Daryz, did not seem to find it difficult at all.

“Look, we’re breeders,” she said, “and you get to the point where you’re taking a risk every time you run the horse. Would we want him to train on for another year? I’m not sure. I think he has other things to do.”

For many of those at Longchamp on a memorable Sunday afternoon, it will be a frustrating decision at best. For those who prefer the winter code it could further support the regular claim that Flat horses are never around long enough to earn true folk-hero status.

Daryz, after all, did not run at two and seems set to retire – like many Classic-winning three-year-olds – after a couple of seasons on the track. Although two Arc victories is a huge achievement, a third would be unprecedented and secure Daryz a place not just among the great Arc winners, but in the conversation about the greatest of all. Having seen off the best from the 2026 Classic crop, a fit, fully mature five-year-old Daryz would surely be a very short price to see off the best of 2027 next October.

Set that against the small risk of a serious injury while racing and it could seem inexplicable not to tilt for racing immortality. France Galop, the sport’s governing body, does not publish detailed statistics on fatal injuries while racing in the manner of the British Horseracing Authority or the Equine Injury Database in the US, but the fatality rate on the Flat in most major jurisdictions is about one for every 1,000 starts. A four- or five-race campaign for Daryz focused squarely on a return to Longchamp would be roughly 200-1 to end with a catastrophic injury.

From a racing fan’s perspective, the risk-reward reckoning of keeping Daryz in training could seem like a no-brainer. From his owner’s point of view, though, the calculation is entirely different since it factors in what would be lost – to the Aga Khan Studs breeding operation most obviously, but also to the sport as a whole – in the unlikely event the worst were to happen.

Princess Zahra’s family has been breeding and racing thoroughbreds since the third Aga Khan, her great-grandfather, made his debut on the British turf in the early 20th century. Hers is the fourth generation to own an Arc winner – there have now been nine in the famous silks – but the first to own a dual winner of the race.

It is worth remembering that Aga Khan Studs is not a commercial operation in the manner of, say, the Coolmore Stud in Ireland. It has five stallions on its roster, sends few of its home-bred yearlings to the sales and still operates in many respects like the traditional owner-breeders that were the bedrock of the turf from its earliest days until the Coolmore-led transformation towards a full-on commercial model in the 1970s.

On that basis, Daryz’s value to the operation goes well beyond what can be summed up on a balance sheet. For his owners, the decision to send him off to stud is every bit as clearcut as the choice to race on at five might seem to be to Daryz’s supporters in the grandstand.

But while the fans and Longchamp seem sure to be denied the spectacle of Daryz lining up for a third Arc, another abiding memory of Sunday’s action, alongside the winner’s brilliant surge to victory, is of a race and an event that has rediscovered its confidence and poise.

In the first couple of years after its €150m rebuild, there were plenty from Britain and Ireland – who account for at least 25% of the attendance – saying “never again” as huge queues for toilets, food concessions and betting windows spoiled their days.

But there were no queues – that I could see, at least – on a half-hour walk around Longchamp in the hour between the Prix de l’Abbaye and the Arc itself. The weather – not just warm, but hot – undoubtedly added to the general air of contentment and allowed the crowd to spread out and explore the space, but the sense of a special day in the sporting calendar was back.

Daryz will be elsewhere on the first Sunday in October next year, but many, if not most, of those who were there to see him win his second Arc may well have it inked into their calendars already.

While there is clearly a need to regulate sheds as much as any other development, the capacity of neighbours to take offence at pretty much anything knows no bounds. And while many are happy if the full force of the law (or the local council) is brought to bear on their neighbours’ “monstrous” intrusion, they will also complain bitterly if their sunlounger or potting shed falls foul of the same regime.

Trying to manage these disputes might be why some planners leave the profession in frustration. Paul BurtonEmeritus professor of urban management and planning, Griffith University, Brisbane, Australia

Emily Retter fails to mention that garden sheds are increasingly being used to house Airbnb guests, with all the intrusions and friction that that can bring. Planning laws need to get to grips with what happens at the back of houses, rather than adopt an “it’s at the back, so what does it matter?” approach. Joyce CorstonEast Molesey, Surrey

Medicine shortages will result if drug prices are driven too low

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 16:50:19 GMT

Amanda Cole says the government needs to weigh the cost of medicines against the damage that a shortage can cause to the NHS and patients

Without decisive government action, the reported medicine shortages in hospitals will only be the tip of the iceberg (Hospitals in England hit by shortages of common drugs such as paracetamol, 29 September). Medicine supply chains are complex and global, with multiple points of potential failure that are especially sensitive to geopolitical shocks. Brexit has made us even more vulnerable, as we no longer have access to EU medicine reserves, and cross-border logistics are further complicated.

Our research shows that these shortages tend to be concentrated in (off-patent) generic and biosimilar markets. It’s true that low prices for off-patent medicines are important in driving health system savings and promoting affordability. The problem is that when prices are driven an unsustainable low, manufacturers exit, leaving markets with too few suppliers and dangerously exposed to any supply disruption or demand spike. The NHS bears the cost when a shortage does occur, in the form of higher prices, expensive substitutes and a heavy staff burden in managing emergency procurement and, sometimes, rationing. Patients pay the highest price in delayed treatment and worse outcomes.

The government needs to weigh pricing controls against the costly damage that a drug shortage can cause. The answer lies in using regulatory, pricing and approval decisions to encourage competition and nurture supplier resilience. There is a critical balance between affordability and medicine security that needs to be struck. Amanda ColeDirector, Office of Health Economics

Badenoch is trying to match Farage step for step – but it’s a dance of death for the Tories

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 16:46:33 GMT

At conference here in Birmingham I found a small battalion of centrist remainers with a vision for the Conservative party to come

You can walk all the way from Somerset to Sussex without crossing a Tory-run constituency, if you wish. You could also travel through each of the counties of Wiltshire, Hampshire, Dorset and Surrey without setting foot in Tory lands. They are now mainly Liberal Democrat, and there’s not one Tory MP in all of Oxfordshire.

Is Kemi Badenoch bothered? Everything she does seems cleverly designed to keep those places lost to her for ever as she woos Reform voters, unsuccessfully. The more she leans right, the more she repels home counties moderates. Those Reform voters are not coming back, psephologists say. Without reclaiming the old “blue wall”, there is no hope, ever, of a Tory majority, say both Profs Tim Bale and Rob Ford and just about every political authority you care to ask.

Shooting the breeze at the party’s Birmingham conference, you might never guess the Tories still poll four percentage points below the last election, the worst result since the Duke of Wellington was dismissed in 1830 for rejecting electoral reform and defending every rotten borough.

Spot that Wellingtonian legacy in the interview Badenoch gave ConservativeHome. “I march to the beat of my own drum,” she says. Indeed she does, but out of step with the public, not condescending to care what it might be thinking and allowing no shade of disagreement. Removing the Lords whip from Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s chief of staff, was a deterrent message to anyone taking part in the “festival of ideas” here, a festival of one idea only. Barwell opposed Badenoch’s edict barring any candidate who supports net zero carbon emissions or staying in the European convention on human rights. “I haven’t left the Conservative party. It has left me,” Barwell tweeted plaintively. It has left a great many others, too.

Margaret Thatcher, still holy here, never did that: she had “wets” in her first cabinet and never expelled them from the party. Her ideological obduracy over the poll tax only overcame her later on, and it did for her. But Badenoch is starting out this way. The adulation showered on her by Tories and their press must come from some alternative wonderland where they are not polling in third place at 19%, while their leader, though improved, scores net -15 – compared with Andy Burnham on +7. In polling, more call her “nasty” or “rude” than “strong” or ‘intelligent”.

What demographic is she for? Giving free childcare to parents earning over £100,000 will strike most as a grotesque gesture. Only 4% make £100,000 or more: they don’t think themselves wealthy, but the other 96% of people do. The £700m cost of that policy should go to the dwindling number of deprived two-year-olds getting early years support, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. Already, the children of the best-off are eight times more likely to benefit from funded childcare hours than the most disadvantaged, says the New Economics Foundation. Children arriving at school unready are tomorrow’s Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training). This should have the education secretary, Lucy Powell, rampaging: it’s not about parents, it’s about children’s futures. Badenoch’s pledge to cut some benefits to “subsistence” level deliberately implies the 4 million children below the poverty line are living the life of Riley.

Her responses to Burnham are also out of touch with the times – and even with the Times. While 70% want closer relations with the EU, her party shockingly pledges to rip up any agreement Burnham makes, sabotaging any trade pact on agri-foods or freedom for the young to travel across Europe. Negotiations are at risk of failure if the EU fears Europhobes might ever regain power and reverse it all.

Austerity is still raw in public minds, with overflowing prisons, blocked courts, NHS waiting lists and a million Neets, alongside the housing crisis. What a time for Badenoch to propose £47bn in cuts, with her shadow chancellor now planning even more “in every part of government”.

Instead of beckoning back those moderate-minded home counties, she competes punch for punch with Nigel Farage. Last week, she stripped down the aid budget to £1bn to equal Farage’s policy. Look at their arms race to demolish the civil service: Badenoch started last year by pledging to cut 132,000 civil service jobs, return it to pre-Brexit levels (before all the mundane EU agencies we quit – medicines, chemical safety etc – had to be replicated). Farage was due to cut a mere 68,500 until Danny Kruger upped the ante last month to 250,000 in his “Storm and Sunshine” policy. The latest? The Tories just pledged to kill off the Environment Agency, Natural England and the Climate Change Committee. What do the home counties think of that?

This contest for lowest taxes, smallest state, toughest stance on migrants, harshest welfare cuts and deepest loathing of young people will spiral downwards towards something new and dangerous. Modern British politics has never before had rightwing parties competing as equals. But locked in this dance of death, the politics of bile carries them further from most voters. Tories are dying out: 63 is now the median age of Badenoch’s voters, while Labour’s is 46.

If nothing improves by next conference, the mirage of Badenoch’s rock-solid support will melt away. But what would replace her? Waiting in the wings there is a model of what a Conservative revival might look like – Prosper UK, launched in January.

after newsletter promotion

It tiptoes, praising Badenoch loudly, yet it is running seven events at this conference. That included a small Sunday night rally for electoral reform. It was addressed by former West Midlands mayor Andy Street, now co-chair of Prosper UK with Ruth Davidson It is backed by a formidable array of what was once the One Nation group, now defunct in parliament – or dormant under Badenoch’s rightwards march. No MPs back Prosper UK in public, but the group claims a third of them do secretly, along with 30,000 declared supporters. David Gauke, vice chair, has crept back into the party – he thinks by accident when the membership computer processing his re-application didn’t register he’d been ejected in 2019. In returning, he joined a battalion of remainer luminaries of the centre-right who’d had the whip suspended at the same time, including Kenneth Clarke and Dominic Grieve.

Gauke travels the country speaking to Conservative associations and others. Prosper UK is pro-EU, pro-migration for skilled workers and foreign students, pro-net zero and against the pension triple lock – and Gauke says that “Conservatives should be truth tellers on all these”. But though socially liberal, he’s dry as a bone on fiscal discipline, campaigning for low business taxes, a smaller state and enticing back non-doms – all Hayek, no Keynes. “No one speaks for some 7 million people centre or centre-right,” he says.

Indeed, the country needs a plausibly electable Tory party to put up a fight against Faragism, not a carbon copy of it. If Badenoch is not for turning, to survive it will need to turn her out.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

“All the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” thundered Virgin Media O2. It’s not an unreasonable view of BT’s hurried weekend acquisition of TalkTalk. Once upon a time, TalkTalk was seen as a plucky upstart performing the useful role of irritant to BT’s giant Openreach broadband operation. Now the challenger is being consumed by the dominant player via a pre-pack administration that minimises short-term political headaches.

Here’s the problem, though, with the cosy stitch-up thesis. For all the howls of outrage, it’s hard to see what the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, who gave her blessing by issuing a little-used public interest notice, was supposed to do differently. Alternative approaches, notably a chaotic collapse of TalkTalk without a rescue plan for the customers, risked worse outcomes.

OK, perhaps the worst fears of GP surgeries and hospitals being disconnected at a stroke, and thousands of vulnerable customers losing their internet connection, were overdone. But, in Nandy’s shoes, you probably wouldn’t take the risk. TalkTalk, after all, had had months to find a buyer but failed to land a credible deal even when its retail division and its wholesale unit, PXC, were up for grabs separately.

Disappointed would-be buyers blame the reluctance of BT, as the critical supplier to TalkTalk, to extend financial support to a new ownership vehicle. From BT’s point of view, however, one can see why another private equity backer for TalkTalk wouldn’t feel like an improvement on the last one. As it is, BT will be booking £100m as a non-payment of a debt even as it takes control.

The deep problem here is that TalkTalk – Sir Charles Dunstone’s creation more than 20 years ago – hasn’t been doing much real challenging work of late. After going through the refinancing wringer more times than is healthy, it was a financially distressed company. At the last count, borrowings were in the region of £1.5bn, a staggering sum for a loss-making business with only 1.5 million retail customers and 1 million wholesale ones. Telephony, remember, tends to be a low-margin game even when things are going well.

That is not to say the politicians get a free pass. Successive governments have been told many times by the regulator Ofcom that a “supplier of last resort” regime should be in place in the broadband market, just as it is in energy and water. The logic is simple: in extremis, there should be a way for a government-supported operation to step in to prevent sudden disconnections and look for an orderly permanent solution.

The unavoidable fact, though, is that such a regime didn’t exist with TalkTalk. That glaring hole in the regulatory setup needs to be addressed for future cases. But a weekend arrangement with BT, however objectionable in theory, at least has the advantage of not drawing on a penny of public money.

The medium-term regulatory test will be to ensure BT and Openreach can’t abuse the advantage of gobbling TalkTalk. There was a theatrical public exchange of letters between the BT chief executive, Allison Kirkby, and the Ofcom boss, Dame Melanie Dawes. The former pleaded for regulatory mercy, in effect, for removing a political problem; the latter replied that applying the regulatory framework was a statutory duty.

It’s anyone’s guess how that will work out in practice since the wriggle room would seem to be enormous. But the guiding principle hasn’t changed – wholesale operators need to have access to Openreach’s network on reasonable commercial terms. TalkTalk couldn’t make it pay but that, in the end, seems primarily to be a story of its own perilous financing. Wrapping the business into BT is very far from being ideal – but it’s not the worst pragmatic fudge.

Is the US becoming a nation of cat lovers?

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 16:05:48 GMT

Dogs have long been more popular, but for the first time more households own kittens than puppies. Some believe it’s all down to economics

Name: The kitten index.

Age: The debate has probably raged since animals have been domesticated.

The debate being? Dogs versus cats. Not in a fight, but as in which to get as a pet.

Well, that depends on whether you want a warm, loving, loyal friend that gives you unconditional love … Or a beautiful, non-needy but still loving animal that doesn’t require constant attention and walking … But we’re not having that argument here.

What are we doing? Looking at some interesting new statistics about cat and dog ownership.

I already know this – dogs win, every year. True; in the 2026 UK Pet Food survey, the dog population (15.5m) is slightly ahead of the cats (13m).

Two and a half million ahead! But crossing the Atlantic now …

Still more dogs, surely? I’m thinking Lassie, Toto, Snoopy, Eddie Crane from Frasier … Granted, there currently are more dogs, but maybe not for long. The market research firm Packaged Facts reports that, for the first time since it started looking at this stuff, more US households own kittens than puppies. The ratio reached 1:1 last year, and now it’s 1:0.94.

But that’s just kittens and puppies. Guess what kittens and puppies grow up to be?

Hmm. Have Garfield, Looney Tunes’ Sylvester and Alien’s Jonesy become the hot new pet icons of film and TV? To be fair, it’s less about boom time for cats, more about dog ownership in decline.

Because? Maybe because kittens are a bit like lipstick.

Excuse me? So the lipstick index was a phrase coined in the 00s, referring to the idea that consumers buy less expensive luxury goods in times of economic hardship, such as lipstick instead of, say, an expensive purse.

But the president says the economy’s going great. He also said people were eating cats and dogs, remember. Truth is, the property market is sluggish, because of real estate prices, high mortgage rates and stagnant wages.

But what’s that got to do with cats and dogs? Packaged Facts says homeowners are nearly twice as likely as renters to have a dog.

Bottom line, it’s all about the budget? It calculates the average dog costs its owner $1,300 (£985) a year. For an average cat: $750 (£570). But, writing in the Washington Post, the chief executive of Packaged Facts, Robert Granader, is keen to point out it’s not about cats replacing dogs. “It’s about America becoming more like cats: living in smaller spaces, valuing independence and preferring to be left alone.”

And where the US goes, the rest of us follow? While ratios differ throughout Europe, the UK Pet Food survey actually points to slightly more dogs than cats compared with the last time they published it, two years ago.

Woof! But the UK is facing the same economic global headwinds as the US, so watch this space.

Do say: “Just a goldfish, please, until I’m on the property ladder.”

Don’t say: “Whichever, cat or dog, it’s just for Christmas, right?”

Preppers used to be ridiculed – but we’re all stockpiling now

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 15:47:12 GMT

The UK government urging households to prepare for unknown threats with a three-day supply of food and water doesn’t feel like an overreaction. But is there a bigger plan to go with it?

There is no national food stockpile and there hasn’t been since it was wound up in the 1990s. It feels like a metaphor for the delusions of that era: nothing bad can possibly happen again; no two countries with a McDonald’s have gone to war with each other (according to the journalist Thomas L Friedman, also in the 90s). Now, we all have a McDonald’s and wars regularly disrupt food supplies. The problem with metaphors is you can’t eat them – not even satisfying ones.

For people who remember the second world war, or feel as if they do, there is always enough muscle memory to do topical household stockpiling. My mum kept a trunk of food that was mainly filled with condensed milk in case of a nuclear war, all the way through the 80s. When the Berlin Wall came down, we should have had a ceremonial toffee-sauce-making event where we ate it all, but we didn’t; in 1990, she was stockpiling again, to mark the Gulf war.

The spectre of Y2K saw a large amount of bottled water enter the house, but by then I’d left home. When 9/11 happened, the water had gone off, but it was still fine for washing, apparently, so all she needed was a load of new water – and all that remained for the wider family was to call her mad and occasionally steal her anchovies.

The 2008 financial crash may have brought almost 20 years of roiling turmoil to the world, but the period spent wondering whether the cash would stop coming out of the wall was only a couple of days, during which if you had got your arse into gear enough to buy beans, you would have been considered hysterical. It would be dispiriting to go through all the events since that have made stockpiling seem like a good idea and impossible to pinpoint the date on which having a three-day food stash went from “crazy prepper idea from someone who probably also keeps a crossbow” to “something any sensible person who reads the news and listens to the authorities would do”.

The UK government’s resilience campaign, urging households to prepare for threats unknown, doesn’t feel like an overreaction. But nor does it feel realistic.

A record number of households – one in eight, or one in six with children – experience food insecurity already, which is to say can’t be sure they have enough even without external events. The range of possible disasters is so wide that it’s hard to consider them practically without freaking out: are we planning for crop failures in the UK or for the collapse of the global food supply, which would mean us relying on our own crops? Are we anticipating a hostile foreign act such as a cyber-attack, or something more meat-world?

Power outages, extreme weather, floods – they all seem possible, but none of them seem as if they’d be over in three days. You can see that having a torch would be better than no torch, but a stash of tinned pineapple wouldn’t meet the moment. The advice is to have three litres of drinking water a day for each person, but can you seriously imagine having that and not sharing it? There is no household solution that doesn’t hinge on the emergency being very short-lived and a collective response being ready to go within only a few hours. The more you think about emergencies, though, the less likely they seem to be short-lived. The chance of inoculating yourself household by household seems vanishingly small.

The essence of old-school prepping – the reason people who did it were mocked and viewed with suspicion – was that it was implicitly off-grid, or rather planning for a world without a grid and without meaningful order. The modern preppers’ problem is that stockpiling for your own household – even having a workable first aid kit and some non-perishables – feels ridiculous unless you believe there’s a bigger plan under way. The government has the unenviable task of asking us to trust the future less while trusting its authority more. It’s enough to make you want to do something helpful – more helpful, even, than buying a gigantic bag of rice.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

Women suffer more pain than men across the whole body, major global study finds

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 15:47:00 GMT

Researchers looked at pain around the world and across the human lifespan, finding steepest rise happens before age 55

Women report suffering more pain than men, a major new global study has found.

That was true for all types of pain the researchers measured, and comes amid continuing concern about the gender pain gap, which means women are less likely to be prescribed the pain relief they need.

Researchers from all over the world carried out “one of the largest harmonisation efforts in pain epidemiology to date”. Data was collected from more than 6 million people from 118 countries from 1990 to 2025, and included people from aged five years to more than 100.

The research, published in Nature Medicine, looked at how pain, as the leading global cause of disability, was distributed both around the world and across the human lifespan.

It found women’s self-reported pain across 11 bodily sites – head, face, neck or shoulder, foot or ankle, hand or wrist, elbow, chest, back, stomach or abdomen, hip and knee – was higher than for men.

That was particularly true for headache, facial and abdominal pain.

For men and women, the steepest increase in pain happened before people turned 55, then peaked at or beyond 75, with back, hip and knee pain increasing across the lifespan.

That indicated “that a substantial share of lifetime pain burden develops during working-age adulthood”, the authors wrote.

About 40% of participants reported back pain, while facial pain was the rarest at 2%.

Those in the lowest Human Development Index regions had substantially “higher late-life prevalence of bodily pain”, and almost twice the rates of low back pain in their older age.

High-intensity pain peaked at about 50, while generalised pain peaked around 70.

“Overall, our results suggest that, although the likelihood of experiencing any pain rises steadily with age, the most disabling forms of pain followed an inverted-U trajectory, peaking in mid-to-late adulthood before declining,” the study authors wrote.

“This distinction, between pain accumulation and pain that intensifies and then resolves, has direct implications for where prevention and care should be concentrated across the lifespan.”

The authors wrote that current estimates focus on diagnoses, which may mean people with limited healthcare access are left out, which is why they analysed rates of self-reported pain. That could provide a foundation for more equitable monitoring and prevention efforts, they wrote.

“Trajectories varied markedly by phenotype: headache, abdominal and facial pain peaked earlier in life before declining, whereas musculoskeletal pain generally rose progressively with age,” they wrote.

“Within musculoskeletal sites, upper body pain (including neck, shoulder and elbow) peaked around midlife and declined thereafter, whereas lower body pain (including back, hip and knee) continued to increase across the lifespan, consistent with the greater role of cumulative mechanical and degenerative load at weight-bearing sites.”

The study found 18.3% of the global pain burden was due to smoking, obesity and low household incomes. This ranged from 12.6% in sub-Saharan Africa to 27.1% in eastern Europe.

In Oceania, 6.6% of pain was attributable to smoking compared with 2.5% in sub-Saharan Africa and 8.5% in eastern Europe, while 11.2% of pain was attributable to obesity, compared with 2.7% in central and southern Asia and 14.6% in North America. And 8% was attributable to lower incomes, compared with 6.6% in sub-Saharan Africa and 8.6% in eastern Europe.

The authors noted that there were important limitations on the research which could affect interpretations but did not alter the overall patterns. Those limitations included different ways of measuring pain, uneven coverage across different regions and oldest and youngest age groups, and that they described patterns for particular age groups, rather than following the same people over time.

Professor Andrew Horne, the director of the Centre for Reproductive Health at the University of Edinburgh in the UK, described the research as a landmark study, showing that women experience more pain than men at every body site studied.

“Pain also rises most steeply before age 55, during women’s working, caring and reproductive years. It is strong evidence that the gender pain gap is real, consistent and global. Yet women’s pain is still too often dismissed, underresearched and undertreated,” he said.

“Closing the gap means taking women’s pain seriously in the clinic, routinely analysing data by sex, properly funding research into the biological and social causes, and developing better, more personalised treatments for women.”

Prof Rebeccah Slater, professor of Paediatric Neuroscience at the University of Oxford agreed. “The troubling paradox is that women experience more pain, yet their pain is also more likely to be dismissed, diagnosed late or undertreated,” she said. “This enormous study shows that the higher burden of pain in women is remarkably consistent across the body and in a remarkably diverse global population.”

US closely monitoring case of lab worker who ‘possibly’ died of plague in Siberia, says Rubio

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 15:36:37 GMT

Quarantine measures in place in several hospitals in eastern Russia amid uncertainty over death of Darya Shipilova

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has said the US is closely monitoring the case of a Russian laboratory worker who died last week after a reported accident at a plague research institute in Siberia.

“We’re watching and monitoring it closely,” Rubio said on Monday before leaving for a trip to Europe. “I ⁠don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an ⁠eye on it.”

Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk, became ill at work. She died two days later on the night of 2 October at a regional hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov.

It remains unclear how she became unwell. Unconfirmed reports in Russian media have suggested Shipilova may have been infected after a mishap at the laboratory. Officials have not publicly confirmed that account.

Local media have reported that the institute has subsequently been locked down, with staff forced to sleep on the floor and on chairs. “They’ve been isolating everybody since Friday – more than 60 people,” one relative, Roman, told the news portal Siberia. Realities.

He said family members were allowed to drop off food at a checkpoint while tests were carried out inside the building. Similar quarantine restrictions have been placed on several other hospitals in and around the city.

Rubio, citing what ‌Russians have released about the death, said it seemed a worker in the lab became ​infected and there was concern the disease may have spread internally.

“There’s very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously,” he said. “But like anything else, something like that gets out, it just quickly spreads.”

Senior Russian officials have added to public disquiet by sending conflicting messages. Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the Buryatia region, which neighbours Irkutsk, initially wrote that Shipilova had died of plague, before editing his post to say she had “possibly” died of the disease.

Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said Shipilova died from “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”. It insisted that tests found no micro-organisms linked to her professional work and described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the area as stable.

Authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk briefly urged residents to avoid travelling to Shelekhov and surrounding settlements after what they said was unofficial information about a possible plague infection. They later deleted the post from social media.

“There are no obvious changes to daily life on the streets, but people are worried and anxious. Locals are angry that they are not being told anything,” said Elena Trifonova, a journalist with People of Baikal, an exiled Russian media outlet specialising in Siberia.

Despite the lack of a confirmed diagnosis, precautionary measures appear to have been introduced across the region. The US-funded Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported on Monday that several hospitals in Irkutsk had been placed under quarantine.

The outlet confirmed that staff from Shipilova’s workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, had been kept inside the institute since 2 October.

Patients at Irkutsk city clinical hospital No 1 and the Ivano-Matreninskaya children’s hospital said relatives were not being allowed to visit and people inside were not permitted to leave.

On social media, local residents described some of the precautions being introduced.

Ulyana Gavryunina, who went on Monday to one of Irkutsk’s main maternity hospitals for a routine check-up on Monday, said doctors refused to allow her mother in, citing a quarantine imposed over the suspected plague case. Gavryunina said staff member checked her for flu-like symptoms and asked her to fill out a screening form for infections, on which “plague” was listed. She posted a photograph of the form on Instagram.

Elsewhere, a mask requirement was introduced at the Irkutsk aluminium smelter in Shelekhov. The plant’s director, Artyom Fominykh, called it a preventive measure, saying: “Better safe than sorry.” Over the weekend several public events in Irkutsk were cancelled.

Shipolova’s death has prompted intervention from senior federal health officials. Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor and the country’s chief sanitary doctor, travelled to Irkutsk on Friday.

She attended an emergency meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission over what officials called a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infection”.

Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, urged residents to remain calm after meeting Popova to coordinate the response. “All identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, none is showing signs of illness and laboratory tests have returned negative results,” he wrote on Telegram.

Kobzev made no reference to reports that a laboratory worker had died.

US politicians have raised concerns about the incident, which follows longstanding and unfounded allegations by the Kremlin that Ukraine has secretly carried out biological weapons research with the support of Washington.

A Republican representative, Don Bacon, a senior member of the House armed services committee, wrote on social media: “I remember hearing from anti-Ukraine voices about their so-called bio labs. It was Russian disinformation ops at their best. But in reality it is Russia with the bio labs.”

Plague remains endemic in parts of Siberia and the Russian far east, where the bacterium persists naturally among wild rodents and their fleas.

But human cases in Russia are rare. Before the suspected Irkutsk case, the country’s last recorded human infection was in 2016, when a 10-year-old boy in Siberia’s Altai Republic contracted plague after helping butcher a marmot.

“This case here seems like a rare lab accident and is unlikely to go much further,” Prof Ian Jones, a professor of virology at the University of Reading, in the UK, said. “Although it is true that pneumonic plague is directly transmissible, the contacts of the primary case are known and can be treated if they show any sign of infection.”

He added: “Plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia, but the living conditions associated with previously spread plague are no longer generally true, antibiotics are available and its potential is therefore limited.”
