Ronaldo’s break with Portugal is sad, fitting, and long overdue

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 15:30:46 GMT

The star’s rift with Jorge Jesus is an unfortunate affair. But the forward has been holding his national team back for years

Sign up for our free newsletter here

If this is to be the end for Cristiano Ronaldo at international level, at least it can be said that he left the stage as he bestrode it: with monumental self-regard. Ronaldo has always been a preening, self-absorbed player, but for a time, when he was one of the best in the world, it could be tolerated. For the past four years, though, he has actively and obviously held Portugal back. There is a great generation of technical talent here weighed down by the monstrous albatross of his ego.

To recap the basic details of the past couple of weeks. Ronaldo played 67 minutes of Portugal’s scratchy 1-0 win over Wales. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, who replaced Roberto Martínez after the World Cup, said he had a verbal agreement with Ronaldo that he would not start the following game against Norway but would perhaps come off the bench. Early in the second half, Ronaldo went to warm up – although whether that was on his own initiative or because Jesus had told him to is unclear. The game was tight, Portugal ultimately winning 2-1, and Jesus did not bring Ronaldo on.

To Ronaldo and his army of apologists, Jesus was guilty of an unacceptable provocation. Jesus’s view was that winning the game took priority over the extremely delicate feelings of a 41-year-old forward. Ronaldo walked out on the squad, and perhaps on his international career, although only three days later, seemingly after Jesus had refused to pay penance for his blasphemy. Which is sad, although perhaps not quite in the way Ronaldo thinks it is.

It’s possible Jesus, who also coached Ronaldo at Al Nassr, could have handled the situation differently. He is not, it’s fair to say, a diplomat. After Martínez’s soft-pedalling, that is, though, perhaps exactly what was needed. Jesus is 72. His vision of management is old-school, which is to say that he is a dictator and he takes orders only from the club president, and then only if he feels like it. His career has been characterized by rifts with players who have resisted him. In a sense the only surprise is that his falling out with Ronaldo took until the second game of his reign.

Others might have been cowed in the face of Ronaldo’s sulk, the online backlash and criticism from some of the Portuguese press, certain elements of which Ronaldo owns, but not Jesus. He is a man of great eloquence and is always quotable but, even by his standards, his response to the furore has been remarkable as he has insisted on the primacy of the team over any individual. “I can say to any player that you’re starting on the bench: if I need you for 30 minutes you’re going to play, if I don’t need you, you’re not going to play,” he said. “The way I was reading the game he didn’t come on. Because it’s not Cristiano, just like it will never be any player that will change my ideas as the coach. Never! Not him, not anyone in football. Not him, not anyone, not any president. Never! Zero!”

His hardline approach might have backfired had Portugal then lost to Denmark, but they won 4-2, playing superbly. Gonçalo Ramos, who might have thought he had already settled this argument by replacing Ronaldo at the 2022 World Cup for the last-16 game against Switzerland and scoring a hat-trick in a 6-1 win, set up the first and scored another against the Danes, having already scored the winner against Norway. “The new manager is a great help,” Ramos said. “We have clearer ideas; we know exactly where each teammate is, both in defense and attack. We’re improving day by day, and it’s all part of a process. We’re very happy with the win, once again against a good team.” Ramos was on target Sunday as Portugal came from behind to beat Norway at home, making it four wins out of four in this window.

The tendency until now has been for the other Portugal players to back Ronaldo, to insist he was an icon and that they didn’t mind his superannuated lumbering. Bruno Fernandes has been notably diplomatic, but others are starting to break cover. Ramos’s former Paris Saint-Germain teammate Vitinha, for instance, who has seen at club level how beneficial a purge of egos can be, observed that Portugal’s improvement has been “the work of the coach … I think beyond the win, the content of our game was great.”

Jesus has offered Ronaldo another meeting to try to resolve the situation, but the Portuguese football federation seems already to have accepted how the affair will end, beginning plans for a farewell game for the country’s record scorer. Both Jesus and Ronaldo have indicated they will say more this week.

after newsletter promotion

But the truth is that this is a break that should have happened long ago. For three tournaments, Ronaldo has undermined an extremely talented Portugal. This is a sad story. It is sad Ronaldo’s career should have ended this way. But the saddest element is that a great player could be so deluded about his own fading ability that a national team’s hopes and dreams should have been sacrificed to his quest to break goalscoring records.

F1 looks amateurish and incompetent after farcical scenes in Sepang

Formula One has gone to no little pains this season in insisting the new format is more popular than ever, despite overwhelming disapproval from the drivers regarding engine regulations. In short, there is nothing to see here.

But the farcical scenes that accompanied the opening to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on Sunday were all too visible and left some drivers expressing open mockery.

Max Verstappen won the race, held at Sepang to replace the cancelled Bahrain GP. It was a dominant drive for his first win of the season, but overshadowed by the sport – that styles itself as the pinnacle of motor racing – looking at best amateurish and at worst incompetent.

The race was delayed because of heavy rain and the track was still very wet as the field lined up for the first time this season in such conditions. They ran behind the safety car to conduct two formation laps before the proposed start.

As they toured round at low speed in low-grip conditions, the engines’ software, now an integral part of the application of power in engines using an almost equal split of electrical and combustion energy, found itself in a scenario beyond its parameters. Chaos ensued. First, Verstappen announced he could no longer accelerate, then Lewis Hamilton slowed and came to a stop before having to do a forced reboot of his car to get moving again. A number of drivers reported the same problem as they crawled around and one Haas and one Cadillac ground to a halt. The field was in disarray and the start had to be suspended.

The problem was caused by a combination of low engine speeds, low grip and the circuit layout coming up against the wet-weather management of the power-delivery software. An unanticipated bug, as the governing body, the FIA, described it. There was a 53-minute delay while the FIA wrote and applied a software update. Verstappen and Hamilton mockingly compared it to the time they had driven in Lego cars as part of the pre-race entertainment at Silverstone in July.

“These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented,” said Verstappen. “When there is some kind of error or glitch, that’s the problem. I triggered it first, then I look in my mirror and I just see everyone … I was, like, wait, are they waiting for me?”

“It was like the Lego race,” said Hamilton. “Yeah, we had the same speed,” said Verstappen. Both drivers were, by now, laughing at the absurdity of the situation.

The FIA said it will conduct a review with the teams and the power-unit manufacturers, but the damage has been done, once more highlighting the foibles of these engines and how much has been taken out of drivers’ control.

Sign up to The Hotspot

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

after newsletter promotion

The debate on the engines has raged all season. Addressing questions about why, for example, battery-usage data was not part of F1’s broadcasts, amid accusations it would demonstrate how hamstrung drivers were by battery management, F1’s chief executive Stefano Domenicali cited a conversation about the sport’s accessibility with the Star Wars creator George Lucas, himself a noted car enthusiast.

“He gave us an incredible chance to see how we can really simplify things because the new fans are not understanding … what is behind the scenes. They are fascinated on the fact there is a lot of action.”

F1 clearly believes the force is strong with its product the way it is and will doubtless point to the fact that when the race did eventually get under way it was an entertaining affair.

Hamilton came back from dropping to 17th to third place, Verstappen was at his imperious best out front, while George Russell’s dramatic late retirement all but put paid to his title hopes.

Yet even the new fans cannot fail to have observed the reality that was laid bare in Sepang: drivers reduced to furiously pushing buttons on a steering wheel, hostages to software over which they have no control, then deriding and condemning the situation afterwards.

Moreover, F1 might also consider it dodged a bullet. Had the race started in the dry and then a downpour arrived, the failure would have happened as the cars circulated mid-race behind the safety car.

The finger should not be simply pointed at the FIA. These rules were agreed with full input from F1, the teams and the power unit manufacturers.

As Carlos Sainz perceptively asked: “My only question is who, five years ago, decided this was the direction to go?”

No quick fix is coming, but what happened in Sepang emphasised how misconceived these regulations were, regardless of how they are perceived by fans of every persuasion.

Aphrodite review – a trashy way to treat the goddess of love

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 14:58:39 GMT

Ashmolean museum, Oxford

She’s the ultimate female nude, a Greek goddess who inspired centuries of artists. Yet despite some world-class loans, her story here is jumbled

Botticelli’s Venus has parked her shell outside your house and come to pay a night-time visit. The glowing strands of her hair glitter against blackness as she looks past you at a mystery only she can see, while your eyes follow those river-like locks down to a hand that gathers a looping cascade between her thighs. She is, unmistakably, the goddess from Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus in the Uffizi, Florence. This very similar painting from about 1490, also by Botticelli and his workshop, suggests his Uffizi masterpiece was already such an icon that someone commissioned this version without the zephyrs and green sea, just that goddess body.

So it goes. Venus, in art, is just a word for “female nude”. Botticelli started a modern appetite that has never ended. From his hypnotic paintings a host of lush sex goddesses rose up, or reclined, to rule European art through to Michelangelo Pistoletto’s ironic 1967 assemblage Venus of the Rags, also here, in which a heap of old clothes overflow from a corner around a marble nude seen from behind, the mix of beauty and chaos resembling a rubbish-strewn Naples piazza.

But this exhibition is not called Venus. And it doesn’t tell her artistic story except in bits with vast lacunae. Instead, it sees Venus as a cheap Roman substitute for the original Greek love goddess Aphrodite, who in turn is exposed as a ripoff of a matriarchal deity once worshipped on Cyprus. The result is a mixture of world-class loans and an archaeological hobbyhorse.

Both the quality and gaps hit you straight away with a classical marble Crouching Venus (sorry, Aphrodite), lent from the royal collection. There’s no exploration of its impact on later art. In fact, this Roman copy of an ancient Greek original was sold by Cromwell’s republican regime after the beheading of its royal owner, Charles I. It was acquired by the artist Peter Lely who painted his own mysterious, nude, anti-Puritan masterpiece Nymphs by a Fountain. After the Restoration he also portrayed Nell Gwyn nude – his interest in this Venus was perversely creative. Before that, Rubens saw this same statue and based his painting Venus Frigida on it.

Which is another way of saying that the story of Aphrodite/Venus in art is massive, epic and complex. Perhaps the comparatively small size of the exhibition can’t hold all that, yet a lot of space is wasted. Still, it has to start somewhere and the first room displays the many ways Aphrodite was depicted in ancient Greece, including a Red-figure vase with a scene of her and rival goddesses, Hera and Athena, preparing for the beauty contest she will win, leading to the Trojan war. So many stories, and this room seems almost breezy with them. The marriage of Aphrodite to the smith-god Hephaestos and her adultery with Ares, god of war, is told in a yada yada way and illustrated by a minor 16th-century print. Then suddenly you are plunged way, way back to encounter what this show claims was the real, original Aphrodite.

In classical mythology, Aphrodite has a special relationship with Cyprus: it is to Cyprian shores that her shell wafts in The Birth of Venus. That is because the Greek Aphrodite, we’re told here, is an appropriation of a female deity who was once all-powerful on the island. Prehistoric totems with abstract bodies, and in one case a bird’s head, attest to the centrality of this cult. Terracotta figures of childbirth and motherhood may have been offered by women to this nameless deity. Other images mix her with Egyptian and Phoenician deities. But I wasn’t convinced that any of this explains the Greek and Roman love divinity. Either way, it is crushingly out of sequence – why didn’t they start here then go forward in time?

What’s inescapable is that the ancient Greeks made nudity their thing. It embodied (literally) their sense of being different from other cultures. But you don’t want to be caught looking too long at the Capitoline Venus. This second-century AD Roman marble statue is a copy of a lost work that was an ancient scandal: the Venus of Knidos by Praxiteles. Before Praxiteles, the Greeks didn’t portray Aphrodite nude, so people were powerfully struck by its intimacy when it was unveiled in the fourth century BC. Aphrodite has stripped for her bath and is trying, failing, to cover herself with her arms. One besotted admirer allegedly entered her sanctuary by night and rubbed himself against the statue’s cold hard thigh, leaving a semen stain.

It’s troubling to see this after you’ve encountered the evidence for the ancient Cypriot Aphrodite. It looks as if the Greeks took a matriarchal deity and turned her into a sex toy. The Romans borrowed that nude image and spread it throughout their empire: a raw, graffiti-like relief from a fort north of Hadrian’s Wall of a naked Venus bathing is a funny, fascinating delight.

For me it’s Botticelli who is the true believer in Aphrodite/Venus. For 1,000 years, ever since the fall of the Roman empire, she was cast out by Christianity. Her worship was revived in the Renaissance. When you gaze at the unfathomable eyes of his Venus, you too believe that love is a holy thing that deserves its own deity.

Aphrodite: The Making of a Goddess is at Ashmolean museum, Oxford from 8 October 2026 to 11 April 2027

I’m sure Daniil didn’t ​want to do this intentionally.”

Spain’s PM Pedro Sánchez calls snap election after housing law fails to pass

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 14:09:31 GMT

Election called after rightwing parties voted down emergency legislation aimed at tackling housing crisis

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has once again staked his political future on a snap general election called after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation to tackle the housing crisis.

Sánchez, who has been in office since 2018, used a televised address to communicate his decision, which had been widely expected. The next general election had been due before the end of next summer.

Announcing on Monday morning that an early general election would be held on 29 November, the prime minister defended his government’s social, environmental and humanitarian record – and admitted it had made mistakes – but said it was time to let the Spanish people have their say.

“It’s up to you now,” he said. “A glance at the horizon shows us that the world is in a very complex era of transformation and transition. It’s a time of great tension, of climate emergency, and of social and technological changes – including highly disruptive advances in artificial intelligence. It is, therefore, a time of great dangers, but also – if we know how to seize the moment – of great opportunities. You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play as well.”

Sánchez’s gamble is being seen as a pragmatic move from a seasoned political risk-taker. His minority coalition government with the small, leftwing Sumar alliance has faced a turbulent time in parliament since the prime minister secured his return to office by striking a controversial deal with Catalan pro-independence parties in the aftermath of the inconclusive snap general election he called three years ago.

Unable to pass a budget since 2023, with his party and inner circle beset by corruption allegations and his government facing enduring pressure over its handling of the mass crossing into Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta over the summer, he appears to have decided another snap vote is his best chance of survival.

Sánchez repeated his familiar assertion in Monday’s address that the choice was between his progressive government and a Spanish right that would curtail freedoms and turn back the clock on hard-won advances.

“You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that rolls back progress wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility,” he said.

“You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society.”

The government’s efforts to tackle the housing crisis were set out in two decrees that contained a range of measures – from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room – but were voted down in congress last Friday by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence party Junts.

The PP, which is leading the polls but which may need to rely on Vox’s support to form a national government, said it believed construction, and not regulation, was the best way to tackle the crisis.

The votes were met with an angry response from the crowds who had gathered outside congress, eliciting boos and cries of “Shame” and “Your profits, our misery”.

The PP welcomed news of the snap election. “At last, the Spanish people will decide,” said the party’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo. “This isn’t an election like previous ones. This is about Spain beating Sánchez.”

Vox, which already governs with the PP in four Spanish regions, hailed the decision. The party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said Vox would fight to ensure that Spaniards “are not discriminated against in their own homeland” when it came to housing and benefits. He also said his party would focus on “remigration” in order to reverse what he called “the migrant invasion”.

Long-brewing fury over the high cost of renting and the precarious nature of many tenancies exploded late last month following the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years. Abascal said she could not possibly afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.

Her plight prompted tens of thousands of people to take to the streets to protest, and saw a huge tent camp reminiscent of the 2011 indignados movement spring up in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square.

Over the weekend, large demonstrations were held across the country as protesters stepped up their demands for urgent action on the housing crisis. Authorities said 70,000 people had taken part in a protest in Madrid on Saturday, while organisers put the figure at 500,000.

Sánchez will be hoping that the focus on housing, and the right’s rejection of his government’s plans to address the crisis, will mobilise voters.

The housing issue has served to deflect attention from the government’s much-criticised handling of the continuing crisis in Ceuta, which was sparked when about 70,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.

Members of Sánchez’s administration, his party and his inner circle have also been battling a series of corruption allegations over the past two years.

In July this year, the prime minister’s brother, David Sánchez, was banned from holding public office for nine years after being found guilty of administrative misconduct relating to his hiring by a socialist-led council in the south-western region of Extremadura.

Meanwhile, Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gomez, is due to face trial after a judge charged her with embezzlement, influence peddling, corruption in business dealings and misappropriation of funds at the end of a two-year investigation.

David Sánchez and Begoña Gómez have both denied any wrongdoing, and the prime minister has previously accused his political and media enemies of launching a “harassment and bullying operation” against his family.

Snakes, bobcats, mountain lions: the secret animal world beneath the Hollywood sign

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 14:00:27 GMT

An international symbol for the city, the sign is also hallmark of the region’s environmental richness

Atop Mount Lee, in the heart of Los Angeles, the wind is quiet. Two red-tailed hawks sail above, barely flapping as they coast the thermal air like surfers on a wave. Standing beside the giant letters of the Hollywood sign, the city seems peaceful. On a clear day, blocks and blocks of homes unfold beneath and the skies reveal sights all the way to Catalina Island – 10 miles out, across the Pacific.

That’s the beauty seen from the Hollywood sign.

The sign sits on a hillside in Griffith Park, which, at about five times the size of Central Park, is the largest municipal park in the city. The letters have long been an international symbol for human residents in the metropolis – of dreams, film-making ambition and success. But it’s also a hallmark of the region’s environmental richness.

Because the area is closed off from the public, it has become a favorite of animals seeking respite from the city. There are birds nesting in the sign, snakes curled up at its base, bobcat roaming around the letters. It was the backdrop that made the famous wild mountain lion P-22 into an LA icon when a 2013 National Geographic photograph captured him prowling at night with the illuminated Hollywood sign in the background.

Now, a team of scientists is preparing to outfit the letters with cameras, able to capture any fire outbreaks that the basin may experience. The sign’s caretakers are collaborating with Torch Systems, a technology company that uses solar-powered sensors, on an AI fire-detection service that can identify smoke from miles away. Fire is considered the area’s largest anticipated risk, particularly as visitors may bring lit cigarettes into the park.

On a recent Wednesday, the Guardian hiked up the mountain with the team to survey the environment of the sign. As we don gloves, skirt a steep trail and rappel down a private trail to the letters, mounds of coyote scat are a constant reminder of who has walked these paths before us.

“Los Angeles is butted up against nature,” says Diana Wright, official caretaker for the Hollywood Sign Trust. She gestures around the hillside, part of the 4,310 acres, or about 6.5 sq miles, that exist in the shadow of the sign. “We’re inside this huge natural park – way bigger than Central Park – and also much more native. And then you’ve got this man-made sign of it that’s meant to withstand rockslides and landslides and winds.”

The park is home to many creatures. The Educational Research Center at the University of California, Los Angeles, has designated Griffith Park a Significant Ecological Area, in part for its crucial role “as a corridor for any gene flow and species movement between the Santa Monica, San Gabriel and Verdugo Mountains”. Researchers have documented about 200 species of birds in the park, along with 50 species of butterflies and 40 species of mammals.

Like many parts of Los Angeles, the sign was originally a publicity stunt – and a temporary one. It was originally constructed of tin and telephone poles in 1923, to advertise a local housing development called “Hollywoodland”. Eventually, the “land” section was dropped. Over the years, the structures deteriorated. Hugh Hefner led a campaign in 1978 to replace the letters with massive steel beams set in concrete foundations.

Over the century, it became a real anchor point for life in the city. Wright points to streetlights in downtown Los Angeles that are designed to resemble New York, and other parts of the city where Parisian city scenes are filmed.

“Much of the city is designed to look like other places due to our filming background,” says Wright. “The sign offers that sense of place that so many parts of the city lack.” She thinks that is why it is often the sign that is blown up in movies – or photographed when something unusual, like a once-in-a-decade snowstorm happens.

The sign may have stronger footholds in the earth now, but it is also facing challenges. Mount Lee is steep, and the hillside, and the animal habitat it is home to faces risks from earthquakes, climate change, changing rainfall and events such as El Niño. The conservancy caregivers have ongoing projects to clear brush to keep fire dangers down, but they have to balance erosion control, fire concerns and unobstructed views of the sign.

Wright and the other caretakers are also developing a plan with the city to plant more native California flora and potentially create a native flower super bloom near the sign. “The Hollywood sign is such a celebration of California,” Wright says. “It should be beautiful and stunning in its natural glory.”

Will the letters still be here in 100 years? And what will the wildlife surrounding it look like then? Wright says it all depends on the land beneath. “The hillside is going to define what the sign is like in the future,” she says, pointing out that the whole city could look different after a big environmental shake-up like an earthquake. “I think that’s a real metaphor for Los Angeles in general.”

But on that day, it was only blue skies and lizards scuttling away from our footsteps, in the shadow of giant letters.

What happens to a dog when its owner can’t leave hospital?

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 14:00:26 GMT

Our relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. But concern for an animal’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcare

“Doctor, do you know I have a little dog?”

My team exchanges a glance. It’s my turn today.

“Tell me about your dog.”

Her face lights up. “Well, he is just a lovely little thing. When I am knitting, he curls up on my lap and keeps me company. We are very happy, the two of us.”

It is unlikely that our patient has knitted in the last year, during which a series of mishaps has brought her in and out of hospital. But the rest of her account rings true.

For as long as possible, she stayed at home, managing miraculously well despite her cognitive impairment, with little help beyond an occasional carer. But now, a fall has brought her undone. For weeks, she has been waiting for residential care, one more statistic in the familiar story of “bed block”.

From our medical perspective, she is waiting for a facility. But from hers, she is waiting to see her dog. She can recall very little about her life but, when it comes to her pet, her descriptions are unwavering. Her words paint a small brown dog, quietly following her around her apartment. Jumping into her lap when she settles into her armchair. Ready to do it all over again tomorrow.

The paramedic who rescued her from her garden noted that the neighbour had offered to take the dog until the patient’s return. But this time, the patient is not going home.

Seeing how much she enjoys the nurses fussing over her – and because she has never once asked to go home – we have not mentioned her living arrangement. But she longs for her dog – and our decision not to lie is far easier in principle than in practice.

There is no easy provision to reunite her with her dog. The neighbour can’t bring the dog in. The hospital won’t let the dog in. (“Imagine the other patients.”)

What if seeing her dog proved distressing afterwards? What if it created a safety risk? And if we made an exception for her, what would we do for the next patient who pined for her turn?

The more frequently I encounter the problem, the more I see it as an emblem of the things medicine considers peripheral to patient care, even when they may not be peripheral at all.

Our relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. They provide physical activity, psychological comfort and social connection. For some older people, an animal is their most constant companion.

But concern for a pet’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcare. Patients may delay seeking care, worry about coming to hospital, or discharge themselves because there is a pet at home.

A recent essay in the New England Journal of Medicine on human-animal relationships points to a perhaps delayed recognition of something we have understood for years: the wellbeing of humans and their pets is intertwined.

When I was an intern, just two questions often formed the social history: Does the patient smoke? Does the patient drink?

Today we do better. We ask: Where does the patient live? What services exist? Is there a history of falls? Is the family involved?

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Perhaps we should add another question: Are you concerned about a pet?

It is a deceptively easy question to ask. Because what happens when the answer is yes?

Who will feed the cat? Who will walk the dog? What if the patient cannot return home?

The solution can’t be another mental responsibility casually added to the medical worklist. Yet ignoring the issue doesn’t obscure the problem.

More of us are starting to notice what we have traditionally neglected – not only where a patient lives but also which animal lives with them and what will happen to that animal if the patient doesn’t go home.

For many people, pets are part of the social determinants of health. Hospitals cannot take on this responsibility alone. But it’s time to ask how hospitals can work effectively with community services and animal welfare agencies to care for the whole patient.

Know thy neighbour – and thy neighbour’s dog.

For as long as we cared for her, one doctor from our team sat down with our patient and heard her retell the story about her dog. We never let our interest drift, even when our hearts slightly broke each time. Every one of us would have brought in her dog – if only we could.

One day, all of us rotated out. We left her in the hands of another team, hoping they would continue the ritual.

Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the Public

Burnham urged to ‘end cycle of harm’ after scale of child-on-child sexual abuse revealed

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 13:56:49 GMT

Nearly 90 organisations write to PM urging him to take decisive action to end violence against women and girls

From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse

A coalition of nearly 90 organisations has written to the prime minister calling for “decisive action” on violence against women and girls after a Guardian investigation revealed the scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools in England and Wales.

The groups urged Labour to redouble efforts to deliver on its manifesto promise to halve violence against women and girls (VAWG) and “end this cycle of harm once and for all”.

Guardian analysis of police data for 2021-25 found that an average of close to five sexual crimes against children aged 12 and younger were recorded by police every day in primary and secondary schools in England and Wales.

The figures include reports of almost 2,000 rapes and attempted rapes, which equates to police receiving an average of one allegation of rape at a school every day. More than a third of the rape victims were children under 13.

It also showed at least 8,500 sexual offences against under-13s were recorded by police as having occurred on school premises or nearby between 2021-25, equivalent to 4.7 reported offences a day.

While most of the police reports did not specify the age of the alleged perpetrator, lawyers and experts say they are likely to be fellow pupils. Most of the victims were girls.

The letter to the prime minister said: “The publication of this data once again shines a light on the harrowing reality of sexual violence in education and among young people.

“All children should have the right to access education without facing abuse, and this data is only the tip of the iceberg given that most abuse is unreported.

“For far too many children, particularly girls, their childhoods are adversely affected in what should be a place of safety. And this doesn’t even account for child sexual abuse in the home, which represents the majority of cases.

“We know that sexual violence can devastate victims’ lives, influencing their physical and mental wellbeing, and at school, their attendance, educational attainment and outcomes.”

Awareness of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools has been growing since an inquiry in 2016 by the women and equalities committee established that sexual harassment and violence were endemic in English schools.

Lawyers and campaigners condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse revealed in the Guardian’s research.

The letter to Burnham has been signed by 87 academics and campaign organisations working in the field, including the End Violence Against Women Coalition, Rape Crisis, Women’s Aid, Refuge, the National Education Union and Everyone’s Invited.

“There is a long history of governments being alerted to such crises,” the letter said. “We have women and equalities committee reports dated from 2016 and 2023, mass testimonials from young people via the Everyone’s Invited movement in 2020, and the subsequent Ofsted review, which concluded that every school and college leader should act on the assumption that sexual harassment and online abuse are problems for their children and young people.

“Once we know better, we must do better,” it went on. “These should have been watershed moments that led to meaningful change, and we are urging you to make this difference today.”

A Department for Education spokesperson said: “The scale of abuse and harassment shown in these figures is truly appalling. No child should ever feel unsafe at school, and we are totally clear that every school must take incredibly seriously its legal duty to act on sexual violence and harassment.” They said the education secretary, Lucy Powell, had set out a new whole-school approach to tackle misogyny head-on in the last month.

“Schools will have the practical tools, training and support they need to challenge harmful attitudes and push back against toxic influences before they take hold,” they said.

‘I spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times’: Ron Perlman on making The Name of the Rose

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 13:53:31 GMT

‘When I couldn’t do the spitting scene, Sean took me aside and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all day.” So I let one fly – and kept having to redo it’

I read an article about a curious book that had great reviews in Italy, a murder mystery about monks in the middle ages fighting for the fictional missing part of Aristotle’s Poetics. I said: “This is for me.” Since childhood, I had been fascinated with medieval and religious architecture, and Aristotle’s Poetics is my favourite literary work.

I learned that Umberto Eco, the author, was going to be in France for one night and agreed to meet me at his hotel and that I would drive him to Charles de Gaulle airport. The first thing I saw was his shadow on the hotel staircase, which looked like the silhouette of Sherlock Holmes – Umberto was a man of great humour, and he met me wearing a deerstalker, with a pipe in his mouth. In the car, I asked questions: what sort of shoes would the Franciscans have been wearing? Would the monks have had beards? What colour would the pigs have been? He said: “I don’t know, I didn’t have to write any of that.” I ended up hiring medievalist Jacques Le Goff and seven of his colleagues to make sure we got all the details right – costumes, architecture, liturgy and so on.

I wanted an unknown to play William of Baskerville, the friar who investigates the deaths, and travelled the world to watch plays featuring great actors in their 50s. Meanwhile, agent Mike Ovitz kept calling, saying: “Sean Connery would love to make this movie.” Eventually, there was a knock on my door and I opened it to find Sean with the screenplay under his arm. He said, “Listen, boy …” and started reading. I had goose bumps. The way he said the dialogue was exactly what I’d been hearing in my head while reading the book.

I flew to Vienna to look at paintings by Bruegel the Elder. I wanted to be inspired by the real people of the period, people who had no dentists or doctors, but I did cast some good-looking monks, too. Christian Slater turned up to audition for the young novice, Adso, and said: “I didn’t learn the lines, I got drunk.” The casting director, Mary Jo, was furious and tried to send him away, but he was the one I wanted. He was only 16, but looked 14. It turned out he was Mary Jo’s son. I had three women selected to audition for the part of the nameless girl from the village, but Christian fell in love with the first, Valentina Vargas, as soon as he did a screen test with her, so I never saw the other two.

We built a vast set on a hilltop near Rome for the monastery and village. During the scene at the end where the library tower burns, Sean’s cowl briefly caught fire, and a big piece of real timber fell on Feodor Chaliapin Jr, who played the blind monk, knocking him to the ground. “I’m 80 years old,” he said, “I don’t mind dying. Was the take good?” He went to hospital and we had to change the schedule because he then had a scar.

After four months in Rome, I went back to my production office in Munich and couldn’t find it. I discovered the film’s producer, Bernd Eichinger, in the cellar with his feet on a table. He said, “JJ, I didn’t want to disturb you during the shoot, but I sold the building to help pay for the movie.”

My very first film, Quest for Fire, was directed by Jean-Jacques. I played a caveman. Transforming myself into something completely foreign was an incredibly rewarding exercise and a phenomenal introduction to the world of cinema, so when I read that Jean-Jacques had attached himself to The Name of the Rose, I went through the book and found a character named Salvatore – an intellectually challenged hunchback who spoke in a jumble of seven languages – who would embody a similar challenge. I told Jean-Jacques that this part would be a dream come true.

Jean-Jacques gave me complete freedom to figure out my dialogue. The Name of the Rose had been published in 80 languages, so I got copies in the seven that Umberto Eco has Salvatore referencing, and circled every time Salvatore spoke. Then I just went, “Eenie, meenie, miny, moe – OK, this word is Latin, this word is Spanish, this word is Italian …” and so on. That was the genesis of Salvatore’s communicative skills.

I worked with a dialect coach who was also a historian with particular knowledge of the period. He suggested the lullaby that Salvatore sings when he’s burned at the stake. Jean-Jacques had this idea that Salvatore was so out of touch with reality that he was initially amused to be in that situation. The lullaby gave a sense of childlike wonder at the fact he’s involved in this ceremony, but doesn’t realise he’s about to lose his life.

I only had to wear the prosthetic hump once, filming the scene where Salvatore is about to be tortured by F Murray Abraham as the inquisitor, Bernardo Gui. I was in the makeup chair for more than 13 hours and by the time I got to set, they had almost run out of time. My hair was shaved so it looked like I had mange. They said: “Good luck with your personal life, my friend.”

I spent every moment I could with Sean Connery, watching him act and listening to his stories. He was my hero, the real deal. When it came to the scene where I had to spit in his eye, I just couldn’t do it. Sean took me aside, and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all fucking day.” So I finally just let one fly. The problem was, you don’t film from just one angle, you have to recreate in profile, medium shot, closeup, over-the-shoulder … I must have spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times that day.

The Name of the Rose is available now on digital and limited edition 4K UHD and Blu-ray (Second Sight Films)

McDermott wants those who ‘can best stick to gameplan’

Hull KR’s Lewis in but no Wakefield players included

Brian McDermott, the England head coach, has justified his surprise decision to omit Jake Connor from England’s Rugby League World Cup squad by insisting the players selected are better suited to his plans to defeat the world’s best.

For the second consecutive year, Leeds Rhinos half-back Connor is the major talking point in a squad that has no players from the new Super League champions, Wakefield. He was left out by Shaun Wane for last autumn’s Ashes despite winning Super League’s Man of Steel award. England lost that series 3-0 after a string of limited attacking displays.

Connor has been in impressive form this year for Leeds, but once again he has been overlooked. McDermott has made no secret of his desire to introduce a more off-the-cuff and exciting brand of rugby rather than attempting to go toe-to-toe with Australia and New Zealand, and has selected Hull KR’s Mikey Lewis rather than Connor.

He did not shy away from explaining why Connor did not fit his philosophy. “We can’t do the usual things,” he said. “We’ve got to play with a point of difference. I’ve got a squad of players of how I want England to play. Jake Connor missed out on selection by a small margin, it came down to who I think can best stick to the gameplan.”

Lewis has been one of Super League’s best players in recent seasons, but he had a disappointing year for Hull KR in 2026, punctured by off-colour performances and disciplinary problems. But McDermott appeared to suggest he can get the best out of the half-back.

“Mikey still won a World Club Challenge with Hull KR and guided them to a cup final this year,” he said. “I get he wasn’t in the best of shape in the back of the year and incurred a couple of bans, but I’ll point everyone to the attack plan and the game model I think England needs to have to compete with the bigger nations.”

Matty Ashton, AJ Brimson, Ben Currie, Zach Eckersley, Herbie Farnworth, Ethan Havard, Max King, Morgan Knowles, Mikey Lewis, Jez Litten, Junior Nsemba, Brad O’Neill, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley, Hugo Savala, Harry Smith, Morgan Smithies, Luke Thompson, Sam Walters, Ben Talty, Jack Welsby, George Williams, Dom Young

McDermott has been hindered by a number of withdrawals, not least from Wakefield. It is understood they would have had four members of their squad on the plane to Australia this week: winger Tom Johnstone, half-back Jake Trueman and forwards Mike McMeeken and Caleb Hamlin-Uele, but they have opted to undergo post-season surgeries. “I’m really disappointed, it’s a real shame the Wakefield boys aren’t available,” he said.

There are further significant absences across the backline in Rhinos’ Ash Handley and Wigan’s Jake Wardle. That has led to surprising call-ups for Australian-born players including Brisbane Broncos forward Ben Talty and Sydney Roosters’ utility Hugo Savala, who will now probably start at centre against Tonga in England’s first game of the tournament in Perth on 17 October.

To state school alumni starting university, I say this: be proud of your background

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 12:22:39 GMT

Accusations of classism chime with my experience 20 years ago. So all hail the Bristol graduate awarding state schools red plaques

“So, where did you go to school?” On the face of it, it doesn’t seem like a loaded question. I was mostly bemused when I first started university 20 years ago and found myself being asked it repeatedly by other students. Why were they so interested? Surely no one would have heard of the north Wales comprehensive I had attended? When they countered my baffled reaction with “Charterhouse” or “Marlborough”, how was I supposed to respond? When one student said, of another, “He went to Winchester, you know”, I stared blankly at him, not understanding why he was telling me about someone else’s day trip to a city in Hampshire (“Oh, did he have a nice time?”). It was strange, new territory.

Asking someone where they went to school is often not an innocent question. It is a way of “placing” you on a social scale. As thousands of freshers settle in to their first terms at university, a significant proportion will be battling with this dawning awareness that Britain runs on a network of private schools whose alumni often seem to know, or know of, one another. State-school students might have been dimly aware of it before, but nothing puts it into sharper focus than freshers’ week. It’s clear that little has changed since my own student days. I was saddened to read recent reports of classism at St Andrews, which led to a student’s announcement that she would not return this academic year: “Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” she said. The pervasiveness of private school culture, as I suppose you could call it, remains nationwide and deeply embedded.

It’s a shock, as a young person, to go from being the majority – state-educated – to suddenly feeling like the minority, and in some stark cases being made to feel “less than” as a result. It’s why I admire Sophie Pender’s 93% Club so much. Pender set up the initiative while she was at Bristol University, where she was mocked for her working-class background, to bring renewed focus to the fact that the vast majority of people educated in the UK – 93% in fact – attended state school, and to offer them a professional career mentoring and networking alternative to the “old boys” that is a de facto benefit of private school attendance.

Pender’s new campaign, Made in State School, aims to shift attitudes by issuing red plaques to celebrate some of the nation’s finest state school alumni – from David Attenborough and Jacqueline Wilson to Jessica Ennis-Hill and Marcus Rashford. She even presented a plaque to Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference last week. She is right when she says that state schools have a PR problem. They are often framed, in rightwing media especially, as dystopian, rough, a hardship that has to be overcome, as opposed to what they actually are: symbols of British excellence, innovation and creativity.

So often the media conversation takes the default assumption that private schools are inherently better than state schools, and that it is always in a child’s best interests to attend one. When you hold opinions like mine – that in rejecting the local state school, you are choosing a form of segregation – they can sometimes feel uncomfortable to express. My industries, media and publishing, are dominated by people who went to private school (half of newspaper columnists are privately educated). Education is a sensitive topic, and this can sometimes have a silencing effect.

So allow me to lay my cards on the table. Sending your child to private school encourages them to believe that they are better than other children. We have seen where this leads, in the behaviour of some of our leading politicians. The cultures of abuse that have been able to thrive at boarding schools that prioritised reputation and prestige over safety have left many victims in their wake.

We should be lauding the benefits of state schools. Being more socially mixed, they teach children openness and confidence. Being able to interact with people from a huge range of backgrounds is a vital life skill. State school kids are often hilarious – there is a unique sense of humour that comes from inclusion; from having seen it all. In the case of mixed-gender schools, they give you a far more developmentally appropriate understanding of the opposite sex. Perhaps due to a combination of socially repressed poshness or a lack of exposure to girls, the ex-public schoolboys at my university often seemed genuinely terrified of the working-class young women they were now expected to study alongside.

I wouldn’t go as far to say that it’s impossible to be cool and to have gone to private school, but let’s be honest, it’s harder. University was the first place I went where privilege was a status symbol, and it was discombobulating to be treated with derision by someone who wouldn’t have lasted two minutes in the roasting competition that was your morning registration. Well, you might say, “cool” shouldn’t matter – but as the Made in State School plaques demonstrate, cool people often go on to do radical, groundbreaking, culture-defining things.

I won’t rehash some of the toxic attitudes I experienced that first term, mostly from public schoolboys, but the scales fell from my eyes. Someone with less confidence and weaker politics might have put on a voice and tried to fit in. Which is why I want to say to any university fresher who feels that way now to hold their head high. These people’s parents chose to purchase educational advantage for their offspring – which was their prerogative – but that doesn’t make them better than you. You’ve still ended up in the same place, without the astronomical costs of private school tuition fees and largely off your own back! Being made in state school is something to be proud of. Become comfortable owning it, and using it to lift others up. We’re the 93%, after all.

Is your partner on their phone and ignoring you? I’ve got a buzzword for that

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 10:00:53 GMT

From microcheating to quiet quitting to weaponised incompetence, new terms to describe relationship failings are abundant. But that doesn’t mean there’s not space for some more ...

Are you committing “attention infidelity”? The New York Times alerted me to this expression, coined by the public opinion researcher Daniel Cox in a new book on the “crisis of human connection”. It’s exactly what you’d expect: failing to focus fully on your partner because you’re indulging in what the NYT calls, rather judgily, “the banal distraction of dead-eyed scrolling”. Who are you calling dead-eyed? This reel of an armadillo in a paddling pool has my animated attention!

Surely we’re all a bit attention-unfaithful – only saints don’t sometimes absent-mindedly thumb through medieval manuscript hedgehog memes while their partner relates a boring anecdote about how they thought they saw a strange bird that turned out to be a plastic bag. What I find more interesting is how we seem now to need a lexicon of relationship bad behaviour.

This summer, there was debate around what constitutes “microcheating”; last year, I read about women “quiet quitting” relationships; the “mental load” has been striking chords for a couple of years, with its companion concept of “weaponised incompetence”. It’s reminiscent of the proliferation of negative phrases around work that emerged post-pandemic – resenteeism, fauxductivity, coffee badging, polygamous working (quiet quitting, of course, also originated in the work context). Maybe it reflects the fact that relationships are also (hard) work, or maybe we just love a bit of pop psychology.

Assuming it’s the second, I’ve been trying to think up other highbrow phrases to conceptualise the age-old business of being a bit of a dick to your partner, so that I can turn them into a book myself. So far, I’ve invented “cultural pre-emption betrayal” (sneaky solo viewing of the next episode of a show you’re watching together), “premium resource caching” (hiding good food), “semi-hostile infantilising” (telling your partner how to do something with the exaggerated patience you’d show a two-year-old) and “fiscal obfuscation” (when you say something was “not very dear” when it was, in fact, very dear).

I reckon some of these may have legs, but I’ve had to stop for now, because my husband wants to tell me about our energy tariff – time to demonstrate some attention fidelity.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Forty years of the Phantom of the Opera - the show that wouldn’t die: ‘People come back to hear the impossible’

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 07:00:49 GMT

As Andrew Lloyd Webber’s enduring gothic melodrama celebrates its 40th birthday, producer Cameron Mackintosh and cast members from down the years recall what makes it so special

There is something about Andrew Lloyd Webber’s masterly musical The Phantom of the Opera – celebrating 40 years on the West End this month – which seems to take hold of its fans in a special way. For me, it was the show that first sparked my love of theatre and inspired me to work in the industry. Even today, Phantom is still the memory that gets my heart racing as I sit in the stalls, waiting impatiently for the curtain to come up, hoping for an experience just as intoxicating and all-consuming as that very first experience all those years ago.

It’s not just the fans, either. When I talk to a cluster of key creatives, all of whom have a special working relationship with the show, each of them seems a little spellbound by Phantom. Sierra Boggess, who plays Carlotta in the 40th-anniversary production, talks tearfully about the lingering spirits of original director Hal Prince and choreographer Gillian Lynne. Jordan Donica, now starring as the Phantom in the West End, speaks passionately about the power of Lloyd Webber’s music (“It feels like heaven to me”), and John Owen-Jones, who has played the Phantom more than anyone else in the West End, talks tenderly about his long-term history with the show: “I’ve got a picture of me in full Phantom get-up holding my baby daughter. It’s an incredible thing to be part of.”

Then there is producer Cameron Mackintosh who, if anything, seems even more enthusiastic about the show with each passing year. He just about stays sitting in his chair throughout our interview, yet gives the impression that he’s bouncing about the office as we discuss those early days working on Phantom: “Of all my productions, it’s the most beautiful show I’ve ever created, where every individual element contributed to its beauty.”

When Mackintosh and Lloyd Webber first started talking about Phantom in 1984, it was only ever meant to be a fun producing project. The two had enjoyed Ken Hill’s production at Stratford East theatre and, after rummaging around a few charity shops, tracked down a copy of Gaston Leroux’s original novel. They discovered a strange and sinister tale about a disfigured musical genius – with a face like a living corpse – lurking beneath a Parisian opera house (The Palais Garnier), seducing soprano Christine Daaé with the power of his music and causing havoc among the company performing above.

As their research deepened, Mackintosh and Lloyd Webber began to unearth the unique characteristics of their new Phantom. Their new version absolutely wasn’t going to be a gothic horror story in the manner of Lon Chaney’s striking silent movie. And it definitely wasn’t going to be a Rocky Horror Show-esque pastiche. This Phantom was going to be lighter, more beautiful – and a lot more romantic.

It also quickly became clear that the show was going to have to feature the music of Andrew Lloyd Webber. “The score was very much inspired by Sarah Brightman,” explains Mackintosh. “Andrew obviously had a very deep relationship with her at the time [the two were married] and it triggered something really special in her. Lots of people have attempted to do Phantom but Andrew’s music brought an emotional intensity to the show that had never been there before in any other version.”

There was something exciting about the score from the start, but it wasn’t until late in the creative process that things came together: “The show only clicked on the first night of previews. I always describe it, up until that point, as a watch running really slowly. But on that night the audience was completely swept into another world. Maria Björnson’s incredible design, Hal Prince’s brilliant ability to shape pictures on stage; [choreographer and stager] Gillian Lynne inhabiting the real world of the opera house and giving it authentic style. It all came together and looked and sounded as one.”

It is amazing to think of all the little tweaks that led to today’s production, revamped and revitalised during the Covid theatre closures, but still very much the same beast created more than 40 years ago. In the early days of rehearsals, there were big plans to include a lot more animals. Björnson was determined to have a white horse carry Phantom into the lair but perhaps unsurprisingly – despite the ingenuity of the props team – they just couldn’t make it work. At one point, Prince wanted scores of rats scampering beneath the stage, but the manufactured clump of glowing rats proved funny rather than frightening (“Those little red eyes had us in stitches!”). Prince also had his heart set on releasing white doves – played by a flock of seriously unpredictable pigeons – and having them fly up into the theatre boxes above. “It was a lovely idea,” says Mackintosh, his eyes sparkling, “except all they did was fly up to a perch and shit all over the audience.”

The horse, the rats and the beautiful (but messy) white doves were all scrapped and the show was gradually finessed. Yet Phantom still opened to patchy reviews, with the Independent scoffing: “Starlight Express brought the form to the edge of the abyss. The Phantom of the Opera takes it back a few yards, but we’re not out of the woods yet.” Nothing about the first few weeks, months or even years working on Phantom screamed box-office gold: “We never tried to put together the most successful musical,” reflects Mackintosh. “I think if we had tried to do that it wouldn’t have succeeded. It was meant to happen the way it did.”

The idea of something almost karmic behind Phantom’s success comes up throughout my conversation with Boggess, who first played Christine 20 years ago and went on to become a fan favourite. “For me, playing Christine was a dream come true,” she says. “It felt like I was supposed to be there, helping to tell this story. And now here I am playing Carlotta. It feels like it’s supposed to be.”

For Boggess it’s the music, above all, that keeps the fans hooked: “There’s no other score in the world like this. People have to hear this music. It’s like it’s changing something on a cellular level.” The acute technical demands of the score are also part of the show’s appeal. “There’s something dangerous about the music,” she says. “The vocal demand is so great and there’s a romance in that. People come back to hear the impossible.”

There is something about performing in Phantom’s first home, His Majesty’s theatre (formerly Her Majesty’s), that feels particularly special for Boggess: “After all the history I have with this show, I finally get to perform in the place where it all started. And there are ghosts here, too. The spirit world is all around us. I really believe that. They come and help us. It’s so much bigger than us all.”

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

Owen-Jones, who has played Phantom nearly 2,000 times, also believes that the venue itself has an important role to play in the production’s extraordinary performance history. He says the show was originally meant to run at the Palace theatre but Les Misérables – the only musical to have a longer West End run than Phantom – was refusing to close. So Phantom opened in the more intimate Her Majesty’s.

“At the time, Her Majesty’s had the only functioning Victorian understage in London,” says Owen-Jones. “So the team were able to use that for things like the candelabra coming up through the floor. People hadn’t seen things like that in the West End for a long time.” Björnson’s design in this particular theatre is a huge part of Phantom’s enduring appeal: “When people watch Phantom they see this incredible set with all these old scenic elements. Flies from the top. Flies from below. Trap doors. Yet when the actors come on stage for their final bow, it’s just a black box. Maria has put all these incredible elements into the space but in the end there’s nothing to look at. It’s pure theatre.”

Everyone I talk to mentions the simplicity of Phantom’s myth-like story, but also its flexibility. It’s a simple tale but a robust one too, which allows each actor – despite the powerful legacy of Michael Crawford’s haunting inaugural performance – to put his own stamp on the title role. For some that might mean imbuing the Phantom with an air of mystery, but for Owen-Jones the key was always about grounding him in reality: “In my mind the Phantom is a man. He’s not a magician. He’s not a wizard. He’s an incredibly talented engineer who can do all these magical things.”

Donica, who began his stage career playing Raoul on Broadway, sees the Phantom through a very different lens: “I felt a kinship to Phantom my whole life. Being a mixed-race kid, raised by a single mum in the south and Indiana. Moving around all the time and being the new kid. The outsider. The person that’s always underestimated and made to feel unwelcome in a lot of spaces; having to show a talent that deems me worthy to be a part of society. All of these things and more, for me, very much relate to Phantom.”

Donica describes the very first time he encountered the Phantom in the theatre, when a touring production came through Indiana. The actor had just turned nine and, in some strange way, he could literally see the power that Lloyd Webber’s music held over the audience: “We were sat in the orchestra level and you hear the Phantom before you see him. I remember hearing ‘Brava, brava, bravissima!’ and it was like a synesthetic response. I could just see the Phantom’s voice hovering over the audience and wrapping around them.”

As we talk, Donica cannot help bursting into song. He talks to me about the frequencies contained in the score and, “from a hertz point of view”, the way that these frequencies connect with the audience. It’s an interesting and unusual way to think about the show; almost as if Lloyd Webber’s score is the result of some sort of physics experiment, designed to shock and move us: “The frequencies that Andrew uses in this show are what hit you to your core. You can sit there, being sceptical about the show, but when you hear those tones – ‘Da-da da-da daaaaa!’ – it automatically makes the hair on the back of your neck stand up. That’s why it works.”

The Phantom of the Opera is at His Majesty’s theatre, London, to 13 March 2027.

Pasture lives: the rebel cheesemakers preserving an Alpine tradition

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 06:00:49 GMT

A story of storico ribelle, produced by a small group of mountain herders according to a traditional farming system based on seasonal and rotational grazing

My journey into the world of storico ribelle began with a shared passion for photography and the mountains. A close friend of mine lives in the Orobie Alps. He loves the mountains and the natural environment that surrounds him, and we share the same passion for photography. When I finally went to visit him, I discovered a way of experiencing the mountains that was very different from the one I knew growing up in the Apennines, where I come from.

What struck me was not only the landscape, but the relationship people still have with it. Here, I discovered a world where the mountain is not simply a place to visit or explore, but a place to live and work. A world where cheese is still a tradition rather than an industrial product, and where the rhythms of the seasons, the animals and the daily work of the alpeggiatori – the mountain herders – are still deeply connected.

There was a poetry in this way of life that immediately inspired me. Waking before sunrise, milking, making cheese, moving with the animals and working until darkness: there was almost no separation between life and work.

I felt compelled to photograph this world. I wanted to tell the story of people who continue to choose a demanding way of life in a time when agriculture is increasingly industrialised and traditional knowledge is disappearing.

In the Orobie Alps, cheese is inseparable from the landscape that gives it life. Steep pastures, stone shelters and seasonal migration have shaped a rural culture for centuries. Animals move with the seasons, milk follows them, and cheese becomes a way of preserving a way of life.

Storico ribelle was born from this tradition – and from a decision to defend it. For generations, bitto cheese was made in small Alpine dairies and exchanged locally for essentials such as grain and salt. During summer, herders moved their animals progressively higher, following the pastures. Along the routes, calecc – simple stone shelters – were used for milking and transforming fresh milk into cheese. The wheels were taken to mountain cellars, or casère, where they could mature for years.

In 1996, the introduction of the bitto DOP (protected designation of origin) brought new regulations. Some producers considered the requirements incompatible with the traditional Alpine system they wanted to preserve. They chose to continue making cheese according to their own methods, outside the DOP. Eventually, a new name emerged: storico ribelle, or historic rebel.

The name reflects resistance, but the deeper story is one of continuity: preserving a relationship between livestock, pasture, milk, cheese and mountain life. That relationship can still be found across Val Gerola, Valtellina and Val Brembana.

At Alpe Pedena, Oreste Pedrelli, 56, has spent the last 10 years herding. He has been making cheese since he was eight, learning the craft from his grandparents. At Alpe Ancogno Soliva, Carlo Duca works with his brother Luigi. Their cheese is renowned for its extraordinary ageing potential, with some wheels maturing for up to 10 years.

At about 2,000 metres, Trona Vaga is the highest storico ribelle Alpine pasture. Manuele, born in 1988, runs the pasture with his partner, Erica, who came to cheesemaking from a completely different background. She studied languages and taught herself the craft as an adult.

Their stories reveal that tradition can be inherited, but it can also be chosen. This is particularly important among a younger generation. Michele Sassella, 15, continues the practice with his mother and sister in memory of his father, Alfio, who dedicated his life to protecting mountain breeds, natural farming rhythms and Alpine biodiversity.

Davide Peregalli, 16, has spent his summers at Alpe Vesenda since he was eight. Gioele Pedercini, 17, has already completed three summer seasons as an Alpine herder while studying agriculture. Valentina, 20, brings another perspective: with a degree in agricultural studies, she is the young cheesemaker at Alpe Orta Soliva.

They represent a generation that is not simply inheriting tradition, but deciding whether it has a future.

That future is fragile. Climate change is already affecting the tradition: scarce rain, increasingly violent storms, and pastures turning yellow even at high altitude. At the same time, increasingly demanding regulations make small-scale cheesemaking more expensive and labour-intensive. Yet the work continues.

Quality here comes with an extraordinary human cost. It means waking before sunrise, working throughout the day and going to bed after sunset. Every hour follows the animals. Milking, often by hand, is followed by transforming fresh milk into cheese. There is little distinction between work and life.

Storico ribelle represents more than a product. It is the result of pasture, animals, knowledge and time – and of people willing to resist the disappearance of a world.

The rebellion began with a choice not to follow a prescribed system. Today, its future depends on another choice: whether a new generation will continue to climb the mountain, care for the animals, make the cheese – and keep alive a way of life that exists almost nowhere else.

‘I didn’t know what to do’: collapse of providers of high-end digs leaves students in shock

The Guardian Mon, 05 Oct 2026 05:00:47 GMT

Cost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodation

“It was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust.

“I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved.

Her sudden upheaval was emblematic of the wider crisis in student housing. While UK universities face a financial crisis, providers of accommodation are grappling with falling international student numbers, a cost of living squeeze and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties.

A string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA), targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty.

It had been touted as the ultimate student living: smart city centre blocks with gyms, cinemas and rooftop terraces have sprung up across the UK. A world away from the traditional image of dirty and dingy shared digs, the flats have offered a spacious alternative for their relatively affluent residents – often international students. Now, some sit half empty, and several schemes have gone bust.

Sriwiboonrattan was among nearly 70 students in Dundee who were left scrambling to find accommodation in late July after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a 116-room city centre block that had a concierge and a shared games lounge with a pool table.

Despite the boom in housing developed by financial institutions in recent years, many students heading off to university this term faced a different dilemma. Rents at the tower blocks have grown much faster than maintenance loans for British students, leaving PBSAs financially out of reach.

Meanwhile, the cost of living crisis has put financial pressure on students seeking university-owned or managed accommodation, while rising rents have hit those wanting to live in shared private rentals. Underlining the scale of the shortage of affordable housing, the students’ union in Bristol included an emergency support number for the housing charity Shelter in an email to new students.

At PBSAs, the national average rent, excluding London, is £191 a week including bills, according to the website StuRents.

At the top end, en suite rooms in Manchester command a weekly rent of £170 to £320, whereas in London, en suite rooms are £250 to £650 a week, and studio apartments in Bloomsbury cost between £550 and £800 plus.

“I wasn’t able to get into PBSA because it is very expensive in Birmingham,” says Soham Chougale, 23, a student at University College Birmingham. “I am an international student, so my working hours are capped at 20 hours [a week in term time], which means I can’t afford to live in PBSA,” says Chougale, the education officer at UCB Guild of Students.

He lived in university-owned dorms for the first two years of his aviation management degree and now shares a two-bedroom privately rented flat with a friend. On campus, he paid £660 rent including bills a month during the first year, which rose by 10% in his second year; now he pays £700 rent a month, excluding bills.

While living on campus “gave me the best feeling of community” and “I still have those friends that I met on the first day”, the wifi was patchy, some facilities were broken and there was a mouse infestation, he recounts.

“PBSA can be quite pricey,” says Matthew Pointon, a real estate analyst at Capital Economics, but adds: “Normally professionally managed buildings are better in terms of quality.”

In London, which attracts the richest students, there is still demand for upmarket accommodation, but outside the capital, there is an oversupply in some cities, such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham.

This week, university staff began strikes in Dundee, Edinburgh and Nottingham over budget cuts, with the industrial action threatening to wipe out a term of teaching for many students.

In Nottingham, demand has fallen from a pandemic peak of 46,295 beds in 2022-23 to 42,290 beds in 2025-26, while 7,700 more PBSA beds came on to the market, the student housing charity Unipol calculated.

The number of students arriving from China has stagnated, and those from the new growth countries India, Pakistan and Nigeria are much more cost-conscious than the pre-Covid students from China, says Martin Blakey, an adviser on student living and the former chief executive of Unipol.

Deniz Yalçın, the chair of the Newington-Meadows branch of the Living Rent union in Edinburgh, says: “In Edinburgh, we’re seeing an explosion of PBSA despite the fact that this type of development is not needed and actually fuels the housing affordability crisis here.

“Many of them lie empty during most of the year, using the Fringe [festival] to bolster profits. Some have even been bought by the council to become temporary housing.”

Richard Ward, the head of research at StuRents, says the key issue is the big gap between maintenance loans and rents, after double-digit rental growth at PBSA blocks and shared houses in recent years.

Maintenance loans have declined in real terms because of below-inflation increases and frozen parental income thresholds. “And what have we seen? More students commuting,” Ward says. “Outside of London, you’re talking about £300 rent a week to make a new PBSA scheme viable. Well, your average British student is paying about £160 a week.”

Occupancy rates at the tower blocks range between 71.3% in Glasgow, 69.9% in Coventry, 89.7% in Bristol and 95.3% in Exeter, as of August, according to StuRents.

Student housing providers are increasingly focusing on the cities with the best universities. Unite Group, the UK’s largest developer and manager of student accommodation, has stepped up sales of unwanted sites.

The loss-making group aims to slim down its portfolio to 55,000-60,000 beds in 20 cities compared with 72,000 beds in 29 cities at present, “to increase alignment to the UK’s strongest universities, where student demand is robust and growing”. Unite reduced rents and tenancy lengths in Nottingham, Leicester and Sheffield, the “most challenging” cities, earlier this year, and rooms start from £99 a week in Coventry.

About 95% of new student beds are being built in cities with Russell Group universities, up from 81% last year, according to the property agency Knight Frank, by investors such as Blackstone, KKR and Greystar. The Russell Group is an association of 24 established UK universities including Cambridge, Oxford, Durham, Edinburgh, Manchester and King’s College London.

Smaller PBSA operators are struggling, with average occupancy levels of 85% across the sector, Unipol estimates. The housing association Sanctuary has been trying to sell student assets of more than 5,600 beds, across 21 properties in eight locations across the UK, for nearly two years, and in July said the buyer had “sought to revisit pricing assumptions” citing changes in economic and market conditions.

Investors poured £164m into the PBSA sector between April and June, one of the lowest quarterly levels on record, although total investment of £2.3bn in the first half was ahead of 2025, according to Knight Frank research. Only 13 deals were completed during the second quarter.

In response to the sector’s headwinds, several PBSA owners plan to rent some floors to young professionals, while one block in Leeds that is only 50% full could partly be used for short-term hotel stays.

In Dundee, Sriwiboonrattan has found alternative accommodation – a studio in the nearby Parklands block – which has a sky lounge with city views, gym and rooftop terrace – where she is paying weekly rent of £240, with financial support from her family. At Marketgait, she says the “walls were thin” with noise coming in from neighbours and lifts unreliable, so she prefers her new surroundings now the initial shock has dissipated.

Others still face a bleak picture, with the freshers’ week parties fading into the memory and the academic year now in full swing. Lewis Wilson, the vice-president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says: “The whole system is broken around student finance and student loans. Some students are going homeless, some students are relying on food banks.” A quarter of student unions now provide a food bank or food pantry.

Wilson, who graduated from the University of Sussex two years ago with a law degree, argues that PBSAs need to be better regulated, and become more affordable. “For the students on lower incomes like I was, I would never have been able to afford a PBSA,” he says.

The government says: “We expect higher education providers to consider the supply, and affordability of student accommodation in relation to their anticipated student intakes and across all years of study at least five years ahead.

“Recognising the inherent uncertainties in student demand and housing delivery timelines, providers should engage with the local planning authority on need.”
